knowledge_points.label: Linear attention: Q(KᵀV) replaces (QKᵀ)V when the softmax is dropped
knowledge_points.statement: Standard attention is quadratic in sequence length because of QKᵀ (n²·d_k FLOPs); if the nonlinearity ρ is the identity, matrix associativity lets you compute Q(KᵀV) instead, and the cost drops from n²d_k + n²d_v to 2·n·d_v·d_k, linear in n.

Cost of attention rises with large context sizes… how do we control those costs?

misconceptions.belief: Linear attention is an approximation of softmax attention that gets the same result faster.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It is exact only when ρ is the identity (or a kernel feature map); with the softmax in place QKᵀ must be materialized because the row-wise normalizer depends on all n scores. Dropping ρ changes the model, not just the algorithm.

predict.q: You keep the softmax ρ but reorder to Q(KᵀV) anyway. Compared with softmax attention, what does the output do?
choices: identical output, just computed faster by reassociating
a different function: linear attention, not softmax attention
a close approximation, with error that shrinks as d_k grows
identical output, but only when n is smaller than d_k
predict.answer: a different function: linear attention, not softmax attention
distractor_from: 'identical output, just computed faster' <- misconception: 'Linear attention is an approximation of softmax attention that gets the same result faster.'
'identical only when n < d_k' <- plausible: mistakes the n-vs-d_k cost crossover for an exactness condition
predict.why: Associativity applies to the product QKᵀV; the softmax sits between QKᵀ and V and does not commute with the reassociation. The slide's condition is 'when ρ is the identity'.
predict.targets_misconception: Linear attention is an approximation of softmax attention that gets the same result faster.

transfer.q: n = 8192 tokens, d_k = d_v = 128. Using the slide's two counts (n²d_k + n²d_v vs 2·n·d_v·d_k), by what factor do FLOPs fall when you switch to Q(KᵀV)?
transfer.why: Quadratic: 2·n²·d = 2·8192²·128. Linear: 2·n·d² = 2·8192·128². Ratio = n/d = 8192/128 = 64. The saving is exactly the ratio of sequence length to head dimension, so it grows with context.

retrieval.q: Which product makes standard attention quadratic in n, and what is its FLOP count?
retrieval.answer: QKᵀ, costing n²·d_k (plus n²·d_v for the product with V).

retrieval.q: What condition on ρ makes Q(KᵀV) a legal rewrite, and what is the resulting FLOP count?
retrieval.answer: ρ is the identity; cost 2·n·d_v·d_k.

prompts.self_explain: Why does the saving factor come out as n divided by d rather than depending on n alone?

steps.do: QKᵀ is n × n, each entry a length-d_k dot product: n²d_k.
steps.why: Every query meets every key, which is the quadratic term. The slide counts multiply-adds, so matmul-flops' factor 2 is dropped on both sides of the comparison.

steps.do: (QKᵀ)V is (n × n)·(n × d_v): n²d_v. Total n²d_k + n²d_v.
steps.why: The n × n matrix is then multiplied by V, so the second product is quadratic in n too.

steps.do: Drop ρ and move the parentheses.
steps.why: Matrix products are associative, but only when nothing sits between QKᵀ and V; with a softmax there the reordering computes a different function.

steps.do: KᵀV is (d_k × n)·(n × d_v): n·d_k·d_v. Q(KᵀV) is (n × d_k)·(d_k × d_v): n·d_k·d_v. Total 2·n·d_v·d_k.
steps.why: No n × n object appears, so n enters only linearly; d is in the thousands while n can be in the millions (video 7:33).

presentations.notice: The two FLOP curves cross at n = d; past that the linear form wins by a factor of n/d, which keeps growing with context.
listen for: why n·d_v·d_k beats n²·d_k: d is thousands, n (the context) is millions

knowledge_points.label: Recurrent form: S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ makes linear attention an RNN
knowledge_points.statement: Linear attention can be written as the recurrence S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ, y_t = q_tᵀ S_t, so the same model has a parallel quadratic form for training and a serial linear form with constant-size state for inference; weighting S_{t-1} by a decay γ gives RetNet.

anchors.quote: This is linear time (great) but the even nicer thing is that this looks like a RNN.
This ‘duality’ allows us to train efficiently (using the parallel, quadratic form) and inference efficiently (using the serial, linear form)
(Note: if one weights 𝑆𝑡−1 by 𝛾, you get a RetNet)
As I sweep left to right on my context, I can multiply my Ks and Vs, and I can update this thing S, which is a state, and I can add it to my previous state.
RNNs are quite nice, because at inference time, I have this S, which is my state, it's fixed in size. ... So RNNs are very nice for inference reasons. ... They are not nice for training reasons.
And then after that, this linear form to this recurrent form, this equivalence, that is exact.

provenance.filtering_note: The recurrence S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ and y_t = q_tᵀ S_t is display math (scattered glyphs in the text layer). The slide does not say what the state S_t is (a d_k × d_v matrix, i.e. KᵀV accumulated over the prefix) nor contrast its constant size with a KV cache that grows with t; that comparison is this thread's supplement supp-kv-cache-bytes. 'Train in parallel' is asserted, not shown: the chunked algorithm that makes the parallel form causal is in the cited papers. Spoken evidence (9:06-9:34): why the duality matters: RNNs are 'very nice for inference reasons' (a fixed-size state carried forward) but 'not nice for training reasons'; linear attention gets 'the best of both worlds'. Spoken evidence (20:48-21:36): a student asked why adding recurrent layers costs quality if the forms are equivalent; the answer: the linear-to-recurrent equivalence 'is exact', the loss comes from dropping ρ, and gated recurrences such as Gated DeltaNet are not equivalent to softmax attention at all. Spoken slip or elision (9:41): 'Unfortunately, this is linear, which is not very good', said right after praising the linear form, while slide p5 says 'This is linear time (great)'. He most likely means plain linear attention is not expressive enough, which is how the next part opens ('linear attention is too naive and simple for me', 11:13); not imported. The state's size is not said aloud either.

prerequisites.note: The recurrence is the causal, per-step version of Q(KᵀV).

misconceptions.belief: Because the model is an RNN at inference, it must also be trained step by step like an RNN.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The duality means the same function has a parallel form Q(KᵀV) over the whole sequence; training uses that, inference uses the recurrence. The two forms compute identical outputs.

predict.q: At decode step t = 100,000, how much state does the recurrent form of linear attention need to keep per head to produce y_t?
choices: one d_k × d_v matrix, independent of t
t vectors of keys and t vectors of values
a t × t score matrix
predict.answer: one d_k × d_v matrix, independent of t
predict.why: S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ accumulates everything about the prefix into a fixed-size matrix; y_t = q_tᵀ S_t reads only that. That is why the slide calls the serial form efficient for inference.
predict.targets_misconception: Because the model is an RNN at inference, it must also be trained step by step like an RNN.

transfer.q: You add a scalar decay so that S_t = γ·S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ with 0 < γ < 1. By the slide's note, which model family is this, and what happens to the influence of a key-value pair seen j steps ago?
transfer.answer: RetNet; its contribution is scaled by γ^j, so old pairs decay geometrically instead of accumulating forever.
transfer.why: Unrolling the recurrence gives S_t = Σ_j γ^{t-j} k_j v_jᵀ. Plain linear attention is the γ = 1 case where every past token keeps full weight, which is the expressivity problem the gated variants on the next slides attack.

check.q: A decayed linear-attention layer updates S_t = γ·S_{t−1} + k_t v_tᵀ with γ = 0.95. By what factor is the contribution of a key-value pair written 20 steps earlier scaled in the current state? Give a decimal; type only the number.
check.why: Unrolling gives S_t = Σ_j γ^(t−j) k_j v_jᵀ, so a pair written 20 steps earlier carries γ^20 = 0.95^20 ≈ 0.358. With γ = 1 (plain linear attention) it would still carry weight 1 (p5; RetNet).
check.varies: a concrete decay value and distance instead of naming the model family
check.invariant: the recurrence multiplies older state by γ once per step, so weight decays as γ^j

retrieval.q: Write the two equations of the recurrent form of linear attention.
retrieval.answer: S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ and y_t = q_tᵀ S_t.

retrieval.q: In the 'duality', which form is used for training and which for inference, and why?
retrieval.answer: Parallel quadratic form Q(KᵀV) for training (whole sequence at once); serial linear recurrence for inference (constant state per step).

prompts.self_explain: Why can a fixed-size matrix S_t stand in for the entire growing set of past keys and values here, when it cannot for softmax attention?

steps.do: Row t of Q(KᵀV) under causal masking: token t reads only keys and values j ≤ t.
steps.why: KᵀV = Σ_j k_j v_jᵀ, and the causal mask cuts this sum to the prefix. The slide leaves the mask implicit, but it is what turns the sum into a running one.

steps.tex: S_t = \sum_{j\le t} k_j v_j^\top = S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^\top
steps.do: Name the prefix sum S_t and update it one token at a time.
steps.why: A prefix sum grows by its newest term, which gives p5's recurrence.

steps.do: The output reads only the state.
steps.why: This is the same y_t as the parallel form, since the step is exact (21:27). Training computes all t at once; decoding carries the fixed-size S forward.

presentations.notice: In the memory panel the green linear-state line stays flat at d_k × d_v however far n moves, while the softmax KV-cache line rises with every token.
With γ < 1 the step-0 pair's weight falls as γ^age along the green curve; at γ = 1 (plain linear attention) it never fades.
listen for: why one model with two forms matters: the parallel form for training, a fixed-size state for inference

knowledge_points.label: Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet: gate the state, then selectively erase it
knowledge_points.statement: Mamba-2 generalizes the linear-attention recurrence with an input-dependent decay γ_t = f(x_t) on S_{t-1} (gating), and Gated DeltaNet adds an input gate β_t and an erase term (I − β_t k_t k_tᵀ) that removes whatever the state holds in the direction of the current key; both keep the parallel/serial duality.

anchors.quote: Let’s generalize linear attention a little bit and add per-position weights..
we can make linear attention more expressive via gating (gating is good!) ... This continues to have duality properties (compute 𝛾 in parallel, apply duality)
Let’s generalize things further – gate the input and selectively erase the state.
The gated delta net adds a ‘no input operation’ gate ... And erases anything in the direction of the current key
Close relationships to various fast weight programming / test time training ideas.
it's important to when to pass information forward and when to just not pass information forward, to forget things and send them to 0.
If beta t is 0, that basically means, don't take any of my current information, don't add it into my state.

not only do I want to put in new information, I also want to erase any previous keys that have gone into it. ... which is essentially acting as a projector that is projecting out things in the kt dimension ... That's not exactly right, because you're not doing things like unit normalization

this acts a little bit like a residual connection, where the value of my current inputs directly pass through to the outputs of my attention. ... And D is another modulated gate, where you can control the amount of pass through that happens.
This update, this projector appears if you try to solve certain kinds of meta learning least squares problems.

provenance.filtering_note: Both update equations are display math (glyphs only in the text layer): Mamba-2 is S_t = γ_t S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ, y_t = q_tᵀ S_t + v_tᵀ D with γ_t = f(x_t); Gated DeltaNet is S_t = γ_t (I − β_t k_t k_tᵀ) S_{t-1} + β_t k_t v_tᵀ with γ_t, β_t = f(x_t). The professor explicitly skips the justification ('There is a lot more words to justify this (go read the mamba 2 paper)') and the SSM derivation; the D skip term is not explained. Why the erase term equals a 'delta rule' (replace the value stored under key k_t rather than add to it) is left to the paper. Spoken evidence (12:18-12:53): γ_t is motivated by LSTM forget gates: knowing 'when to just not pass information forward, to forget things and send them to 0'; β_t is the matching input gate ('don't add it into my state', 16:14-16:39). Spoken evidence (17:01-17:46): the erase intuition the slides leave to the paper: when writing under k_t, also 'erase any previous keys that have gone into it'; (I − β_t k_t k_tᵀ) acts as a projector out of the k_t direction, 'not exactly right, because you're not doing things like unit normalization' (so the delta-rule reading assumes unit-norm keys, as this KP's check does). Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above ('the D skip term is not explained'): at 15:36-16:01 he calls the v_tᵀD term 'basically a residual layer ... not core to the state update', and in Q&A (21:49-22:26) explains it: the current token's value passes straight to the output, with D 'another modulated gate' setting how much. Spoken (17:46-18:21): the projector update was reinvented in meta-learning least-squares problems, fast-weight programming and test-time training (p9's 'close relationships'). Closing remark (22:29-22:52): most tested methods 'converged to almost very LSTM-like objects'.

prerequisites.note: Both variants are edits to the S_t recurrence.

misconceptions.belief: The gate γ_t in Mamba-2 and the gate β_t in Gated DeltaNet do the same job.
misconceptions.why_wrong: γ_t scales the whole previous state (forget everything a bit); β_t scales how much of the current key-value pair is written and how strongly the old content along k_t is erased. β_t = 0 is a 'no input' step, which γ_t alone cannot express.

predict.q: In Gated DeltaNet, a token arrives whose key k_t exactly matches a key stored earlier, with β_t = 1 and γ_t = 1. What happens to the old value stored under that key?
choices: it is replaced by the new value v_t
it is added to the new value
it is unchanged
predict.answer: it is replaced by the new value v_t
predict.why: (I − k_t k_tᵀ) projects out the component of S_{t-1} along k_t (for unit-norm k_t), then k_t v_tᵀ writes the new value there. Plain linear attention would add, producing a blend.
predict.targets_misconception: The gate γ_t in Mamba-2 and the gate β_t in Gated DeltaNet do the same job.

transfer.q: You want a layer that can skip writing anything for a filler token but must otherwise keep its full memory. Which of the two gates on slides 7 and 9 gives you that, and what value do you set?
transfer.answer: The Gated DeltaNet input gate β_t set to 0 (the 'no input operation'); γ_t stays 1 so nothing decays.
transfer.why: With β_t = 0 the erase term becomes I and the write term vanishes, so S_t = γ_t S_{t-1}. Mamba-2 has no way to suppress the k_t v_tᵀ write except by scaling the whole state.

check.q: In Gated DeltaNet with γ_t = 1, the state holds the scalar value 4 under a unit-norm key k. A new token arrives with the same key k, value 10 and input gate β_t = 0.5. After the update, what value does reading the state with query q = k return? Type only the number.
check.why: The erase term (I − β_t k kᵀ) keeps (1 − β) of what is stored under k and the write adds β·v: (1 − 0.5)·4 + 0.5·10 = 7. β_t interpolates between keeping the old value (β = 0, no write) and replacing it (β = 1), while γ_t would scale the whole state (p7, p9).
check.targets_misconception: The gate γ_t in Mamba-2 and the gate β_t in Gated DeltaNet do the same job.
check.varies: a fractional input gate instead of β = 0, with a numeric readout
check.invariant: β_t controls how much of the current key's slot is erased and rewritten; γ_t scales the whole state

retrieval.q: What does Mamba-2 add to the linear-attention recurrence, and what property does it keep?
retrieval.answer: A per-position gate γ_t = f(x_t) multiplying S_{t-1} (plus a v_tᵀD term); it keeps the parallel/serial duality.

retrieval.q: What two things does the Gated DeltaNet update do that Mamba-2's does not?
retrieval.answer: Gates the input with β_t (β = 0 means no write) and erases the state in the direction of the current key via (I − β_t k_t k_tᵀ).

prompts.self_explain: Why would erasing along the current key, rather than decaying everything uniformly, help a model that must overwrite a fact it stored earlier?

steps.do: Start from the linear-attention recurrence (p5).
steps.why: Every pair is added with weight 1 and never leaves, so the state can only accumulate.

steps.tex: S_t = \gamma_t S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^\top,\quad y_t = q_t^\top S_t + v_t^\top D,\quad \gamma_t = f(x_t)
steps.do: Mamba-2 (p7): an input-dependent decay on the old state.
steps.why: γ_t is a forget gate like an LSTM's (12:24): it scales the whole state at once. D is a gated pass-through of the current value (22:11), not part of the state update.

steps.do: Gated DeltaNet (p9): add an input gate β_t on the write and an erase term on the old state.
steps.why: β_t = 0 skips the write ('no input operation'); (I − β_t k_t k_tᵀ) acts only along the current key's direction and leaves the rest of the state alone.

steps.tex: k_t^\top S_t = k_t^\top (I - k_t k_t^\top) S_{t-1} + k_t^\top k_t\, v_t^\top = 0 + v_t^\top
steps.do: The predict's case: γ_t = β_t = 1 and a unit-norm key k_t equal to a stored key. Read the state along k_t.
steps.why: k_tᵀ(I − k_t k_tᵀ) = k_tᵀ − k_tᵀ = 0 when ‖k_t‖ = 1, so the old value is erased and replaced (the delta rule). The professor notes that without unit normalization this is only approximately a projector (17:15).

presentations.notice: β acts only on the slot under the current key: β = 1 replaces the old value, β = 0 leaves it untouched, β in between lands on the line between old and new; γ instead shrinks the whole curve every step.
listen for: the erase intuition: write under k_t and clear out what was stored under that key

knowledge_points.label: Gates that read only the input keep the parallel/recurrent duality
knowledge_points.statement: A gated linear recurrence keeps linear attention's duality (a parallel matrix-multiply form for training, a recurrent form for inference) only if every gate is a function of the inputs alone, such as γ_t = f(x_t); a gate that reads the state, as a classic LSTM's gates read h_{t-1}, forces training to run step by step.

anchors.quote: as long as you're getting the various terms in your RNN, so to speak, with only input-dependent terms, so no state dependence, then you will still have this fairly nice duality between parallel operations, which you can use for training, and serial operations
Gamma of t is not stateful. ... Gamma of t only depends on my current inputs x of t. ... This gamma is not state-dependent at all, so this means that this is very simple to compute.
Attention had the very strong advantage of hardware efficiency. ... I think the reason why the state space models have caught on, despite their similarity to LSTMs

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only as a general rule. Slide p7 says for Mamba-2 only 'This continues to have duality properties (compute γ in parallel, apply duality)', and p9 writes γ_t, β_t = f(x_t) without stating why that matters. The professor states the rule explicitly ('the rule of thumb ... only input-dependent terms, so no state dependence', 14:31-14:56), stresses that γ_t 'is not stateful' (12:40-13:03), and in Q&A (33:01-33:35) uses it to explain why state-space models caught on despite resembling LSTMs: the duality restores the training efficiency that attention used to have over LSTMs. The mechanism (a state-dependent gate cannot be computed before S_{t-1} exists, so the gate products over a span cannot be precomputed) is the author's gloss; the professor gives the rule, not the proof.

prerequisites.note: The gates γ_t and β_t this rule is about.

misconceptions.belief: Any gated recurrence, including an LSTM, can be trained in parallel like linear attention, since it is also a recurrence over a state.
misconceptions.why_wrong: LSTM gates read h_{t-1}, so step t cannot start before step t-1 finishes. The duality needs gates computable from the inputs alone (14:31).

misconceptions.belief: Making the gate input-dependent (γ_t = f(x_t)) instead of a constant breaks the duality.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Input-dependent gates are fine: every γ_t can be computed from x in parallel first and then applied (p7, 'compute γ in parallel'). Only dependence on the state breaks it.

predict.q: You design a new gated linear-attention layer S_t = γ_t S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ. Which choice of decay gate still lets you train it with the parallel (matrix-multiply) form?
choices: γ_t = σ(W x_t), from the current token
γ_t = σ(W h_{t-1}), as in an LSTM gate
γ_t = σ(W S_{t-1}), from the previous state
γ_t = σ(q_tᵀ S_{t-1} k_t), from a state read
predict.answer: γ_t = σ(W x_t), from the current token
predict.why: Only the input-dependent gate can be computed for all positions before the recurrence runs. The other three read the state (h_{t-1}, S_{t-1}, or a read of S_{t-1}), so each step must wait for the previous one.
predict.targets_misconception: Any gated recurrence, including an LSTM, can be trained in parallel like linear attention, since it is also a recurrence over a state.
predict.distractor_from: each wrong option is a gate that reads the state (LSTM-style h_{t-1}, the raw state, a state read), from the belief that any gated recurrence parallelizes

transfer.q: A researcher adds a gate α_t = f(x_t, x_{t-1}) to Gated DeltaNet, computed from the current and the previous token. Does the layer keep its parallel training form? Answer and give the reason.
transfer.answer: Yes. α_t depends only on inputs (x_t and x_{t-1}), which are all known before the recurrence runs, so every gate can be computed in parallel first; no gate reads the state.
transfer.why: The rule is about state dependence, not about how many inputs a gate sees: any function of the input sequence can be precomputed.
transfer.varies: the gate reads two tokens instead of one
transfer.invariant: no gate depends on S or on an output computed from S

check.q: Which of these recurrences can be trained with a parallel (non-sequential) form? f is a small learned network and y_{t-1} = q_{t-1}ᵀ S_{t-1}.
choices: S_t = f(x_t) S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ
S_t = f(S_{t-1}) S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ
S_t = f(y_{t-1}) S_{t-1} + k_t v_tᵀ
S_t = tanh(S_{t-1}) + k_t v_tᵀ
check.why: Only the first gate depends on inputs alone. f(S_{t-1}) and f(y_{t-1}) read the state directly or through the previous output, and tanh(S_{t-1}) makes the update nonlinear in the state; all three must run step by step.
check.varies: surface: recurrence equations instead of gate choices
check.invariant: parallel form exists only when nothing but the inputs enters the gates and the update is linear in S
check.distractor_from: state dependence hidden in a gate, in the previous output, or in a nonlinearity

retrieval.q: A gated linear recurrence computes its gate as g_t = sigma(W s_{t-1} + U x_t), where s_{t-1} is the previous state. How must it be trained, and why?
retrieval.answer: Step by step (no parallel matrix-multiply form), because the gate reads the state, as an LSTM's gates read h_{t-1}.

retrieval.q: Why could LSTMs not be trained in parallel while Mamba-2 can, although both use gates?
retrieval.answer: LSTM gates read the previous hidden state, so each step waits for the last; Mamba-2's γ_t depends only on x_t, so all gates can be computed at once and the recurrence has a matrix-multiply form.

prompts.self_explain: Why does a gate that reads the state force training to proceed one token at a time?

presentations.notice: listen for: 'only input-dependent terms, so no state dependence' as the condition for the duality

knowledge_points.label: Hybrids: a few full-attention layers per several linear/SSM layers
knowledge_points.statement: Production linear-attention models interleave a minority of full softmax attention layers with linear or SSM layers (MiniMax M1 7-to-1, Nemotron 3 and Qwen Next about 3-to-1) and report competitive quality with linear scaling in context length, though controlled ablations of the ratio are scarce.

anchors.quote: Minimax M1 (and minimax-text-01) use a 7-to-1 hybrid (7 linear, 1 full) linear attention.
Performance (generally) seems strong, and they show linear scaling in context length
Mamba attention hybrid (3-1 ish) – comparable (or better) pref to other similar models
The newest qwen are 3-1 GDN / Attention hybrids. ... Once again, pretty reasonable performance with good inference characteristics
Not many controlled ablations, but some evidence of low losses at small hybrid ratios

anchors.ref: Qwen 3.5 / Qwen Next (as named on slide p10)

anchors.quote: It's not fully linear, because you've got these softmaxes, but the dependence is much, much milder.
No one has, thus far, really proven out fully linear time attention mechanisms at scale. ... Everything that I'm going to talk about in the next couple of slides is a hybrid.
Qwen Next has much higher decoding throughput relative to Qwen 3 as the context length goes up and up and up.
You see that at the low ratios, there's basically no hit. ... And then once you pass a certain point, you start to see more significant degradation in long context performance
Single key retrieval is a task that, I think, all of these long context architectures explicitly optimize for.

provenance.filtering_note: All benchmark tables and the hybrid-ratio loss plot (p6, p8, p10, p11) are figures without a text layer; no benchmark numbers or loss values are quoted. 'Linear scaling in context length' on p6 refers to a figure of inference FLOPs/latency vs context. Why some full-attention layers are needed at all (exact retrieval / copying that fixed-size state cannot do) is not stated on the slides; it is the implied reason for keeping a 1-in-N softmax layer. Spoken evidence (10:59-11:11): 'No one has, thus far, really proven out fully linear time attention mechanisms at scale. Everything ... is a hybrid.' MiniMax M1 is 'not fully linear, because you've got these softmaxes' (10:36). Spoken evidence (19:03-20:41): the p11 study is named (ByteDance Seed and UC Santa Cruz) and read aloud: at low ratios of recurrent to full layers 'basically no hit', past a point 'more significant degradation in long context performance', and pure RNN is clearly worse; single-key retrieval flatters these architectures because they 'explicitly optimize for' it, while QA declines steadily. Figure values read aloud: MiniMax M1 competitive with o3 and DeepSeek-R1 (10:22-10:31); Nemotron 3 compared with Qwen3 thinking and GPT-OSS, with good throughput at long context (13:49-14:04); Qwen Next 'much higher decoding throughput relative to Qwen 3' as context grows (18:42). Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above ('why some full-attention layers are needed at all ... is not stated'): it is stated aloud in Q&A (32:50-34:15): the downside of state-space layers is 'expressive power', and with a finite state 'you're going to be losing some information relative to just carrying everything'; see the spoken KP finite-state-recall-tradeoff. Spoken (2:59-3:18): p3's local+global hybrids ('global attention once every eight layers') are the same cost-control idea with local layers.

misconceptions.belief: A model that adopts linear attention replaces every attention layer, so its inference cost is fully linear in context.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Every production example on the slides keeps a fraction of full softmax layers (1 in 8 or 1 in 4), so a KV cache and a quadratic term remain for those layers; the hybrid lowers the constant, it does not remove the quadratic part.

predict.q: A 56-layer model uses MiniMax M1's 7-to-1 hybrid. How many layers still keep a growing KV cache at inference?
predict.why: 7-to-1 means 7 linear layers per 1 full-attention layer, so 56/8 = 7 full-attention layers keep a KV cache; the other 49 keep a fixed-size state.
predict.targets_misconception: A model that adopts linear attention replaces every attention layer, so its inference cost is fully linear in context.

transfer.q: Compare the KV-cache memory of a 3-1 hybrid (slide 8/10) with an otherwise identical all-softmax model at a long context, ignoring the linear layers' small fixed state. What fraction remains?
transfer.why: Only 1 in 4 layers stores keys and values, so the cache is a quarter of the dense model's; a 7-to-1 hybrid would leave an eighth. Quality at these ratios is what slide 11 says is supported by 'some evidence' but few controlled ablations.

retrieval.q: What hybrid ratio does MiniMax M1 use, and what ratio do Nemotron 3 and the newest Qwen use?
retrieval.answer: MiniMax M1: 7 linear to 1 full. Nemotron 3 and Qwen Next: about 3 to 1.

retrieval.q: What caveat does the lecture attach to the hybrid-ratio evidence?
retrieval.answer: Not many controlled ablations; only some evidence of low losses at small hybrid ratios.

prompts.self_explain: Why might a model need any full-attention layers if gated linear attention is already more expressive than plain linear attention?

presentations.notice: Only the blue softmax layers keep a growing cache, so the hybrid's cache is that fraction of the all-softmax one at every context length, and it still grows linearly.
listen for: no loss at low hybrid ratios, then degradation past a point, worst at full RNN

external_prerequisites.note: Interleaving a minority of full-attention layers is the same pattern as sliding-window/full interleaving, with linear or SSM layers in place of windowed ones.

knowledge_points.label: Sparse attention (DSA): a lightweight indexer picks which tokens to attend to
knowledge_points.statement: Instead of replacing attention, DeepSeek Sparse Attention keeps softmax attention but attends only to tokens selected by a very lightweight indexer, which cuts cost and can be adapted post hoc onto a model pretrained with dense short-context attention.

anchors.quote: Instead of attending to every token, do sparse attention (DSA)
The indexer can be very lightweight, giving significant gains ... Can be ‘post hoc’ adapted after dense short context pretraining
DSA – Deepseek Sparse Attention (v3.2, GLM5)

what the indexer does is, it takes the qk inner products, it takes a ReLU. ... And then you're going to take this through a top k, where some number of these top positions get included into my attention computation.
What you do is you just train a normal transformer. ... And when you do your long context extension, you actually then drop in this lightning indexer
it usually goes like short context pre-training, long context extension, then post-training.
you don't lose very much in performance relative to full attention, even at long context retrieval tasks that are fairly difficult to do with RNN style architectures.

provenance.filtering_note: The DSA diagram (p12) and the result figure (p13) have no text layer: the indexer's architecture, how many tokens it selects, and the reported speed/quality numbers are not quoted. The slide frames DSA as the 'alternative to hybrids', i.e. sparsify softmax attention rather than swap in a recurrent layer; the trade-off (still needs a KV cache, but reads only a subset of it) is implied, not stated. Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above (the indexer's architecture and token count 'not quoted'): the forward pass is described aloud (23:49-24:27): the indexer takes the q·k inner products, applies a ReLU, weights them with weights 'derived from the preceding tokens', then a top-k picks the positions that get full attention; k is set near short-context lengths and is 'bounded ... regardless of the input size' (29:45-29:55). No value of k is said. Spoken evidence (24:43-25:09, 28:39-29:39): 'post hoc' means the indexer is dropped in at the long-context-extension stage of the usual recipe (short-context pretraining, long-context extension, post-training), so it adds little training cost; 'it's surprising that it works' with a non-differentiable top-k. Figure readings (25:15-26:42): V3.2 matches Claude 4.5 Sonnet and Gemini 3; prefill and decode costs scale better than the previous DeepSeek; GLM5's ablations lose little even on long-context retrieval 'fairly difficult to do with RNN style architectures'. The trade-off this note calls implied is stated aloud: DSA is not linear time (26:48); see the spoken KP dsa-indexer-still-quadratic. In Q&A (31:50-32:21) he ties the indexer to low precision: select in low precision, then attend in full precision.

prerequisites.note: Presented as the alternative to the hybrid approach.

misconceptions.belief: Sparse attention removes the KV cache like linear attention does.
misconceptions.why_wrong: DSA still keeps every token's K and V so the indexer can choose among them; the saving is in how many are read and scored per query, not in what is stored.

predict.q: You have a dense model pretrained at short context and want long-context inference to be cheaper without pretraining again. Per slide 12, which route does the deck say supports 'post hoc' adaptation?
choices: sparse attention with a lightweight indexer (DSA)
replacing layers with Gated DeltaNet
a 7-to-1 linear/full hybrid
predict.answer: sparse attention with a lightweight indexer (DSA)
predict.why: DSA keeps the pretrained attention weights and only adds a selector, so it can be bolted on after dense pretraining; the hybrids replace layers and are trained that way from the start.
predict.targets_misconception: Sparse attention removes the KV cache like linear attention does.

transfer.q: Compared with full attention at context n, which costs does an indexer-based sparse attention reduce and which does it leave unchanged: (a) KV-cache storage, (b) per-query score computation, (c) KV bytes read per query?
transfer.answer: (b) and (c) fall to the number of selected tokens; (a) is unchanged because every token's K and V must still be stored for the indexer to choose from.
transfer.why: Sparsity is applied at read time. That is the structural contrast with the recurrent alternatives, where storage itself is constant.

check.q: A model switches from full attention to DeepSeek-style sparse attention, where a lightweight indexer selects the top 2,048 tokens per query, at a 128K-token context. What happens to the main KV-cache memory per sequence (leave aside the indexer's own small key cache)? Answer up, down or same.
check.answer: same: every token's K and V must still be stored so the indexer can choose among them; only the scores computed and the bytes read per query fall.
check.why: Sparsity is applied when the cache is read, not when it is stored. That is the structural contrast with linear attention and other recurrent layers, whose state is constant-size (p12-p13).
check.targets_misconception: Sparse attention removes the KV cache like linear attention does.
check.varies: asks only about storage, as a direction
check.invariant: indexer-based sparse attention keeps the full KV cache and reads a selected subset

retrieval.q: What two properties are claimed for the DSA indexer?
retrieval.answer: It can be very lightweight (giving significant gains) and can be adapted post hoc after dense short-context pretraining.

retrieval.q: Which models are named as using DSA?
retrieval.answer: DeepSeek v3.2 and GLM5.

prompts.self_explain: Why does sparse selection avoid the expressivity concerns of a fixed-size recurrent state while still cutting cost?

presentations.notice: In the memory panel DSA sits on the softmax KV-cache line: the indexer cuts what each query reads and scores, not what is stored.
listen for: the indexer's steps: q·k products, ReLU, weights, top-k, then full attention on the subset

knowledge_points.label: DSA is not linear time: a cheap quadratic indexer, then attention over k
knowledge_points.statement: DeepSeek Sparse Attention is still quadratic in context length, because its indexer scores every query against every earlier token; it saves cost through constant factors instead: the indexer is made very cheap (low precision, low dimension), and the full attention that follows costs n·k with k bounded regardless of input length.

anchors.quote: Notice, I'll go back one slide, this is not linear time. ... The indexer still has to operate on full all to all attention ... But you can make this indexer much, much cheaper, for example, by making this lower dimensional or making this w very small.
in order to know what to select, it does have to look at everything. ... It is really brute force inner products.

You can do that in much lower precision, which they talk about. ... So the constant factors are very good. ... even though it's quadratic, it's quadratic on a shorter context length, because it's top k, we can control k.
So regardless of the input size, they would be bounded.
So this is another one of these things of, sometimes, don't get too stuck up on the quadratic versus not.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only. Slide p12 says 'The indexer can be very lightweight, giving significant gains' and p13 shows a cost figure; neither says the indexer is still O(n²) or that k is bounded. The professor says it unprompted (26:48-27:08) and again in Q&A (27:30-28:35), and ends with the course theme 'don't get too stuck up on the quadratic versus not. Sometimes, the constant factors are really, really important', which echoes his FlashAttention remark at 3:21-4:42. He calls the attention step 'quadratic on a shorter context length'; per query it is linear in k, so its total is n·k, which is what the prompts use. No value of k is said (DeepSeek-V3.2 uses 2,048); the numbers in the prompts are illustrative.

misconceptions.belief: Because each query attends only to k selected tokens, DSA makes attention linear in context length.
misconceptions.why_wrong: To choose the k, the indexer scores every earlier token: 'it does have to look at everything ... brute force inner products' (27:40-27:49). Its cost is still O(n²), only cheap per pair.

misconceptions.belief: If the indexer is quadratic anyway, DSA cannot save anything.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Big-O is unchanged but the constants are not: the indexer runs in low precision and low dimension, and the expensive attention runs on k ≪ n tokens (28:01-28:26).

predict.q: Context grows from 64K to 128K tokens while DSA keeps k = 2,048 selected tokens per query. Which part's total cost over the sequence roughly quadruples?
choices: The indexer's scoring of all token pairs
The attention over the selected tokens
Both parts, by the same factor
Neither part, since DSA is linear time
predict.answer: The indexer's scoring of all token pairs
predict.why: The indexer compares every query with every earlier token, about n² pairs, so doubling n quadruples it. The attention over selected tokens is n·k with k fixed, so it only doubles.
predict.targets_misconception: Because each query attends only to k selected tokens, DSA makes attention linear in context length.
predict.distractor_from: linear-time belief (neither part, or only the attention); same-scaling confusion

transfer.q: Same setup: the context doubles from 64K to 128K tokens with k = 2,048 fixed. By what factor does the total cost of the attention over the selected tokens (summed over all queries) grow? Type only the number.
transfer.why: n queries each attend to k tokens, so the cost is n·k; with k fixed, doubling n doubles it (while the indexer's n² quadruples).
transfer.varies: which part of DSA is measured
transfer.invariant: k is bounded independently of n

check.q: A DSA indexer scores all n² query-token pairs at 1 unit per pair. The main attention costs 64 units per (query, selected token) pair and selects k = 2,048 tokens per query. At what context length n do the two parts cost the same? Type only the number.
check.why: n² = 64·n·k gives n = 64·2048 = 131,072. Beyond about 131K tokens the cheap quadratic indexer dominates, which is why making it cheap (low precision, low dimension) matters.
check.varies: surface: find the crossover instead of a scaling factor
check.invariant: indexer cost grows as n², attention cost as n·k

retrieval.q: What part of DeepSeek Sparse Attention is still quadratic in context length, and why does it not dominate the cost?
retrieval.answer: The indexer, which must score every earlier token to choose the top k. It is made very cheap (low precision, low-dimensional projections), and the expensive attention runs only on k tokens.

retrieval.q: Where do DSA's savings come from, if not from a better big-O?
retrieval.answer: Constant factors: a lightweight indexer and full attention over a bounded k ≪ n selected tokens.

prompts.self_explain: Why must the indexer look at every earlier token even though the attention uses only k of them?

presentations.notice: The dashed indexer line climbs with the same n² slope as softmax while the top-k part grows only like n; past n = R·k the cheap indexer is most of the bill.
listen for: 'this is not linear time', and what makes the indexer cheap anyway

knowledge_points.label: A fixed-size state must compress the whole context
knowledge_points.statement: A linear-attention or state-space layer carries the entire prefix in a state of fixed size, so it loses information once the context holds more than that state can store; the only way to avoid the loss is a state as large as the context, which brings the cost back, and this is why production models keep some full softmax attention layers.

anchors.quote: Well, the downside, I think, is expressive power. ... The all to all connection in softmax attention is incredibly powerful.
if you have a finite state and you have to carry everything through, you're going to be losing some information relative to just carrying everything.

if you have a state the size of your context, then you're good to go, but then you're paying these very large costs. ... if you want a really tiny state, it's really hard to compress all the information in a big context.
Basically, at the end, as you go to full RNN, you have very noticeable performance degradation in all these architectures.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only, in a student Q&A (32:39-34:22) and in the commentary on the hybrid-ratio study (19:03-20:41, p11 figure). The slides say hybrids work and give 'some evidence of low losses at small hybrid ratios' (p11) but never say why a softmax layer is kept; the hybrid-attention-ratios note flagged that reason as implied. The professor names expressive power and the fixed state, notes that long-context retrieval is 'fairly difficult to do with RNN style architectures' (26:26-26:42) and that single-key retrieval flatters them because they 'explicitly optimize for' it (20:24). He hedges: 'It might be possible one day to not have any trade-offs' (34:15). The state-versus-cache numbers in the prompts (a d_k × d_v state per head against 2·n·head_dim cached numbers per head) are the author's quantification using supp-kv-cache-bytes; the professor gives no numbers.

prerequisites.note: The hybrids whose softmax layers this explains.
Where the fixed-size state comes from.

misconceptions.belief: Because the recurrent form of linear attention is mathematically exact, a pure linear-attention model loses nothing relative to softmax attention.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The recurrent form is exact relative to the parallel linear form; the lossy step was dropping the softmax (21:17-21:27), and a fixed-size state cannot hold an arbitrarily long context (33:38).

misconceptions.belief: A bigger recurrent state fixes long-context recall for free.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A state as large as the context does restore recall, 'but then you're paying these very large costs' (34:02-34:08); the state is cheap only because it is small.

predict.q: A pure Gated DeltaNet model and a 3:1 GDN/softmax hybrid score the same at 4K tokens. Both are then asked, at 512K tokens, for one fact stated once near the start. Which result is most likely?
choices: The hybrid recalls it far more reliably
Both recall it equally; the recurrence is exact
The pure GDN model recalls it more reliably
Neither can; 512K exceeds any context window
predict.answer: The hybrid recalls it far more reliably
predict.why: The pure GDN model must have squeezed the fact into a fixed-size state along with 512K tokens of other text; the hybrid's softmax layers keep every token's key and value and can look the fact up directly.
predict.targets_misconception: Because the recurrent form of linear attention is mathematically exact, a pure linear-attention model loses nothing relative to softmax attention.
predict.distractor_from: exact-recurrence belief; reversed advantage; context-window confusion

transfer.q: A GDN head keeps a state of d_k × d_v = 128 × 128 numbers. A softmax head with head_dim 128 caches one key and one value (128 numbers each) per token. At what context length does the softmax head's KV cache hold as many numbers as the GDN state? Type only the number.
transfer.why: 2·128·n = 128·128 gives n = 64. Past 64 tokens the fixed state is already smaller than what full attention keeps; at 1M tokens it is about 15,600 times smaller, so it must discard information.
transfer.varies: representation: count stored numbers instead of predicting recall
transfer.invariant: the recurrent state is fixed in size while the KV cache grows with n

check.q: Hold the state size of a pure linear-attention model fixed and double the length of the context it must summarize. Does the state capacity available per context token go up, down, or stay the same?
check.answer: down: the same fixed number of state entries now has to summarize twice as many tokens, so each token gets half as much capacity
check.why: The state does not grow with n, so capacity per token falls as 1/n; this is the compression that costs recall at long context.
check.varies: surface: capacity per token instead of a recall task

retrieval.q: What downside does the professor name for state-space and linear-attention layers compared with softmax attention?
retrieval.answer: Expressive power: a finite state must carry the whole context and loses information, while softmax attention's all-to-all connection keeps everything.

retrieval.q: Why can't you simply make the recurrent state as large as the context?
retrieval.answer: Then you pay the large memory and compute cost you were avoiding; the state is cheap only because it is small.

prompts.self_explain: Why does keeping even one softmax layer in four help a model recall a fact from far back in the context?

presentations.notice: The fixed state and the KV cache cross at d_k·d_v/(d_k+d_v) tokens, a few dozen for typical heads; beyond that the state per context token shrinks as 1/n.
listen for: 'if you have a state the size of your context, then you're good to go, but then you're paying these very large costs'

knowledge_points.label: MoE: more parameters at the same FLOPs per token
knowledge_points.statement: A mixture-of-experts layer replaces one big feed-forward network with many feed-forward 'experts' and a selector that routes each token to a few of them, so parameter count grows with the number of experts while FLOPs per token do not; at matched FLOPs the model with more parameters does better.

anchors.quote: Replace big feedforward with (many) big feedforward networks and a selector layer ... You can increase the # experts without affecting FLOPs
Same FLOP, more param does better
Typical: replace MLP with MoE layer ... Less common: MoE for attention heads
MoEs take advantage of sparsity – not all inputs need the full model
MoEs are most of the highest-performance open models, and are quite quick

anchors.ref: Switch Transformer Fig. 1 (MoE layer) and scaling plot

anchors.quote: One way of thinking about mixture of experts is, they are just a more efficient MLP.
I have 4x the parameters, or at least for my FFN, I have four FFNs worth of parameters. ... But on any forward or backward pass, I'm only going to pay one FFN worth of cost.
if you keep the total compute the same, but you just increase the number of sparse parameters, somehow, the models are generally getting better.
So something like two times faster or something like that, training a MoE relative to a dense model.
MoEs have a lot of parameters. ... It's hard to fit them on a single device.

provenance.filtering_note: The MoE layer diagram (p15) and the same-FLOP scaling curves (p16, Fedus et al 2022) are figures; no loss values or expert counts are in the text. p17-p23 ('Faster to train MoEs' [OlMoE], 'Highly competitive vs dense equivalents', 'Parallelizable to many devices', Qwen and DeepSeek ablations, DeepSeek v3) are result figures that the statement summarizes only qualitatively. The deck never defines 'active parameters' explicitly; the term appears in the p35 table and p54-p56. Memory cost of holding all experts (parameters, gradients, optimizer state scale with total params, not active) is not mentioned on these slides, though it is the flip side of the FLOP claim. Spoken evidence (35:46-36:50): a worked case: four experts each the size of the original FFN give '4x the parameters' but 'one FFN worth of cost' per forward or backward pass; 'this is the mental model that you should have for MoEs'. 'Conceptually, they don't really change the game ... just a more efficient MLP' (34:29-34:40). Figure readings: Switch Transformer test loss keeps falling as experts are added at fixed active parameters (37:36-37:52); OLMoE trains 'something like two times faster' than dense (38:50); Qwen 1.5 MoE with 2.7B active beats many 7B models (41:31-41:44). Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above (memory cost of all experts 'not mentioned'): 'MoEs have a lot of parameters. It's hard to fit them on a single device' (46:26-46:30), and expert parallelism is presented as 'reducing your memory use' per device (42:23). Attention-head MoEs (p25) are 'much less common' and 'haven't been quite as easy to tame' (46:46-47:15), so only FFN MoEs are covered.

external_prerequisites.note: The FLOP claim is only half the budget: parameters, gradients and optimizer state scale with total (not active) parameters.
'Same FLOP' means the 6·N·D accounting applies to active parameters, not total.

misconceptions.belief: Doubling the number of experts doubles the compute per token.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each token still visits only the top-k experts; compute per token depends on k and the expert size, not on how many experts exist. Doubling experts doubles parameters and memory, not FLOPs.

predict.q: An MoE layer has 8 experts, each the size of the dense FFN, and routes each token to 2. You raise the expert count to 64 with the same expert size and k = 2. Per-token FLOPs for the layer change by what factor?
predict.why: Slide 15: you can increase the number of experts without affecting FLOPs. Each token still runs through 2 experts; the router's cost is negligible. Parameters went up 8x.
predict.targets_misconception: Doubling the number of experts doubles the compute per token.

transfer.q: Same layer, 64 experts of dense-FFN size, top-2. Relative to the dense FFN, state (a) the factor on FFN parameters and (b) the factor on FFN FLOPs per token.
transfer.answer: (a) 64x parameters; (b) 2x FLOPs (two experts per token instead of one FFN).
transfer.why: Parameters scale with the number of experts; FLOPs scale with k times expert size. This gap is the whole point of slide 16's 'same FLOP, more param does better'.

check.q: An MoE layer has 128 experts, each 1/4 the size of the dense FFN, and routes each token to 8 of them. Relative to the dense FFN, by what factor are the FFN FLOPs per token multiplied? Type only the number.
check.why: FLOPs per token = k × expert size = 8 × 1/4 = 2 dense FFNs. Parameters are 128 × 1/4 = 32 dense FFNs. The expert count drives parameters; k and expert size drive FLOPs (p15-p16).
check.targets_misconception: Doubling the number of experts doubles the compute per token.
check.varies: fine-grained experts and a larger k instead of full-size experts with top-2

knowledge_points.label: Routing is per token, and experts are not topic experts
knowledge_points.statement: An MoE router makes a separate choice for every token from a single linear projection of that token's hidden state, so the tokens of one sequence spread over many experts and the specialization that emerges is shallow and token-level (punctuation, symbols, non-English scripts), not semantic domains such as medicine or law.

anchors.quote: the scale at which we route experts, is at token level. ... So every token gets an expert.
the routers are super naive. ... They're a single matrix multiply between your input and your whatever. ... You don't know it's like a medical question or not.
because the routers are so simple, it's not like, experts are like smart experts. ... They're not like medical experts, legal experts, or whatever.
punctuations might be routed to one expert or other symbols might be routed to one expert, non-English language character sets might be routed to another expert. ... There's no semantics

The name 'mixture of experts' invites the domain-expert reading this KP corrects.

misconceptions.belief: All tokens of one sequence go to the same experts.

transfer.answer: It contradicts the domain-expert picture: the expert specializes in a token type across all domains. The router sees one token's hidden state through a single linear map and picks per token, so lexical features are what it can separate.

retrieval.answer: Per token; a single linear projection (inner products of the token's hidden state with one vector per expert), followed by top-k.

retrieval.answer: Shallow, token-level specialization: punctuation, symbols, non-English scripts. Not semantic domains like medicine or law.

knowledge_points.label: Why MoEs lagged: infrastructure, heuristic objectives, fine-tuning overfit
knowledge_points.statement: MoEs were slow to be adopted because their infrastructure is complex and their advantage shows mainly in multi-node settings, their training objectives are heuristic and sometimes unstable, and sparse MoEs overfit on small fine-tuning sets (Zoph et al. fine-tune only the non-MoE MLPs; DeepSeek instead uses a large 1.4M-example SFT set).

anchors.quote: Infrastructure is complex / advantages on multi node ... Training objectives are somewhat heuristic (and sometimes unstable)
Sparse MoEs can overfit on smaller fine-tuning data
Zoph et al solution – finetune non-MoE MLPs ... DeepSeek solution – use lots of data 1.4M SFT

anchors.ref: ST-MoE (Zoph et al. 2022), instability and fine-tuning sections

anchors.quote: it's hard to parallelize experts in ways that are efficient in utilization.
They have so many parameters that if you're trying to fine tune the experts, you actually end up with very serious overfitting issues.
especially the attention fine-tuning is something that I see quite often with MoE works recently.
maybe you should just use 1.4 million examples instead of whatever number you have.

provenance.filtering_note: p24 shows a Switch Transformer multi-node speed figure and an ST-MoE instability plot, both without text numbers. p50's overfitting curves (train vs validation for sparse and dense) are figures. The 2026 framing is that these barriers have been overcome: 'MoEs are most of the highest-performance open models' (p20). Spoken evidence (45:33-46:40): adoption came 'only in 2024 onwards' although Google pushed MoEs in 2022; the reasons said aloud are that experts are hard to parallelize efficiently, there are too many parameters for one device, and training 'can really blow up on you'. Spoken evidence, which partly corrects the note above (the professor 'does not say why sparse models overfit more'): he attributes it to parameter count: 'They have so many parameters that if you're trying to fine tune the experts, you actually end up with very serious overfitting issues' (1:18:24-1:18:32). He adds fine-tuning only the attention layers as common recent practice (1:19:01-1:19:12; not on the slide), calls the 1.4M-example SFT 'the bitter lesson version' (1:19:20), and identifies the p50 task as 'one of the glue benchmark tasks' (1:18:48).

misconceptions.why_wrong: The MoE has many more parameters and each expert sees only the tokens routed to it, so slide 50 reports that sparse MoEs overfit on smaller fine-tuning data where a dense model of equal FLOPs does not.

transfer.q: Your team has a 20k-example SFT set and an MoE whose dense layers (attention, non-expert MLPs) are a minority of parameters. Which of the two remedies on slide 50 is available to you, and what does it do to the expert weights?
transfer.answer: The Zoph et al. remedy: fine-tune only the non-MoE MLPs (and other dense parts) and freeze the experts, so the experts' capacity cannot be spent memorizing 20k examples. The DeepSeek remedy needs on the order of 1.4M examples.
transfer.why: Freezing the sparse parameters removes the overfitting-prone capacity; scaling the data instead makes the capacity useful. The slide presents both as solutions to the same symptom.

knowledge_points.label: Top-k token-choice routing: a linear gate, top-k, softmax before or after
knowledge_points.statement: Almost all MoEs use token-choice top-k routing: a logistic-regression gate scores the experts for each token, the top k are selected (Switch k=1; GShard, Grok, Mixtral k=2; Qwen, DBRX k=4; DeepSeek k=7 per slide p29, which matches DeepSeekMoE's small setting of 1 shared + 7 routed experts; the v1 row on p35 is 6 routed + 2 shared, and DeepSeek-V3 routes 8 plus 1 shared), and the gate weights are either softmaxed over all experts then masked (DeepSeek v1-2, Grok, Qwen) or softmaxed only over the selected k (Mixtral, DBRX, DeepSeek v3); expert-choice, hashing, RL and matching-based routing are the alternatives.

anchors.quote: Many of the routing algorithms boil down to ‘choose top k’ ... Token chooses ... Expert chooses ... Global routing via
Almost all the MoEs do a standard ‘token choice topk’ routing.
Switch Transformer (k=1) ... Gshard (k=2), Grok (2), Mixtral (2), ... Qwen (4), DBRX (4), ... DeepSeek (7) ... Hashing ... Common baseline
RL to learn routes Used in some of the earliest work ... Bengio 2013, not common now ... Linear assignment for routing ... Used in various papers like Clark ‘22
Gates selected by a logistic regressor
This is the DeepSeek (V1-2) router ... (Grok, Qwen do this too) ... Mixtral, DBRX, DeepSeek v3 softmaxes after the TopK

anchors.ref: Sparse expert models review, routing taxonomy figure

anchors.quote: You can have the expert choose the token. ... So each expert picks their favorite tokens
So basically, almost all the MoE do token choice TopK.
token choice is going to get lower validation losses, higher downstream benchmark scores compared to expert choice.
This gives gains, not as much as TopK, but somehow, hashing-based expert routing is also something that people do.
the approaches needed to do RL introduce a lot of overhead in terms of both the RL algorithm and the stochasticity.
It's been shown to do good things in some cases, hasn't been seen at scale at all. ... because it's extremely expensive relative to the others to get working.

provenance.filtering_note: The gate equations on p31 (g_i = softmax(Wx) masked to top-k vs softmax over the top-k logits) are shown as an image from Dai et al 2024, so the formulas are not in the text layer; 'softmaxes after the TopK' is the only textual statement of the difference. p28's 'Some recent ablations' refers to a figure (token-choice vs expert-choice) with no numbers. Expert-choice routing is named in the p27 taxonomy ('Expert chooses token') but never defined on the slides: each expert picks its top tokens, which fixes the per-expert load by construction at the cost of variable tokens-per-expert visibility to the sequence. Hashing is listed as a 'common baseline'. The p29 k values are the deck's; DeepSeek's '7' does not match the v1 row of the p35 table (64 routed, 6 active, 2 shared); it matches DeepSeekMoE's small 2B setting of 1 shared + 7 routed experts (confirmed by the p33 figure legend: '1 shared expert + 7 out of 63 routed experts'). Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above (expert-choice routing 'never defined'): it is defined aloud, 'each expert picks their favorite tokens' (48:35-48:42), and global assignment is 'this very complicated router that globally decides' (48:42-48:55). Spoken (49:09-49:46): the p28 OLMoE ablation read aloud: token choice gives lower validation loss and higher downstream scores than expert choice; expert choice 'also trains fine', and perhaps one unreleased Llama 4 model used it. Spoken (50:36-50:59): hashing 'gives gains, not as much as TopK'; a common baseline, not deployed. RL is rare because of the overhead of the RL algorithm and its stochasticity, while heuristics on plain top-k work (51:48-52:16). Linear assignment 'hasn't been seen at scale at all ... extremely expensive' (52:43-52:56). The router is 'a small, small linear projection': each expert has a vector direction and the closest in inner product wins (49:55-50:13); the same top-k pattern appears in DSA and H-Nets (53:05-53:19). The softmax-before/after distinction on p31 is not discussed aloud and no k values are read out.

misconceptions.belief: Softmax before top-k and softmax after top-k give the same expert weights.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Softmax over all N experts then masking leaves k weights that sum to less than 1 (mass leaked to unselected experts); softmax over only the k selected logits renormalizes them to sum to 1. The selected set is the same, the mixing weights are not.

predict.q: A router produces logits for 8 experts; the top-2 logits are equal and the other 6 are much smaller but nonzero. Under 'softmax after the TopK' (Mixtral), what do the two selected weights sum to?
predict.why: Softmax over the 2 selected logits only; equal logits give 0.5 each. Under the DeepSeek v1-2 style (softmax over all 8, then mask), the two weights would sum to less than 1 because the 6 unselected experts take some mass.
predict.targets_misconception: Softmax before top-k and softmax after top-k give the same expert weights.

transfer.q: In the p27 taxonomy, which routing family guarantees every expert processes exactly the same number of tokens per batch without any balancing loss, and what does it give up?
transfer.answer: Expert-choice routing ('expert chooses token'): each expert takes its top tokens, so load is balanced by construction; it gives up the guarantee that every token is processed by k experts (some tokens get more, some none).
transfer.why: Token choice fixes k per token and leaves load free; expert choice fixes load per expert and leaves k per token free. The deck says almost all production MoEs still choose token-choice top-k and fix load with a loss.

check.q: A batch of 256 tokens is routed over 8 experts with expert-choice routing: each expert takes its top 64 tokens. Which statement must hold?
choices: every token is processed by exactly 2 experts
every expert processes exactly 64 tokens
no token is processed by more than 2 experts
every token is processed by at least 1 expert
distractor_from: 'every token by exactly 2 experts' <- plausible: imports token-choice's fixed k (8 × 64 / 256 = 2 is only the average)
'no token by more than 2 experts' <- same confusion: treats the average as a cap
'every token by at least 1 expert' <- plausible: assumes no token can be left out
check.why: Expert choice fixes the load per expert by construction and leaves the number of experts per token free: some tokens get several experts, some none. Token choice is the reverse (p27).
check.varies: concrete batch numbers, and the learner must pick what is guaranteed rather than name the family
check.invariant: token choice fixes k per token; expert choice fixes tokens per expert

More experts, shared experts all seem to generally help
Gains from fine-grained experts, none from shared experts.
Model Routed Active Shared Fine-grained ratio ... Mixtral 8 2 0 ... DeepSeek v1 64 6 2 1/4 ... DeepSeek v3 256 8 1 1/14 ... OlMoE 64 8 0 1/8
V1 (16B – 2.8 active): ... Shared (2) + Fine-grained (64/4) experts

there's some very common processing that I want to apply to all tokens.

it turned out that if you had this classic expert design, you were just reusing a lot of these weights to do common modeling. ... And so you can offload this into the one shared expert, letting these guys specialize even more.

knowledge_points.label: Discrete routing is not differentiable: RL, noise, or balancing heuristics
knowledge_points.statement: Sparse top-k gating is not differentiable, and the three answers are reinforcement learning on the routing policy (works via REINFORCE but high gradient variance and complexity keep it rare), stochastic perturbation of the gate (Shazeer 2017 gaussian noise, Fedus 2022 multiplicative jitter later removed by Zoph 2022) to make experts less brittle, and heuristic balancing losses, which is what practice uses.

anchors.quote: Major challenge: we need sparsity for training-time efficiency… ... But sparse gating decisions are not differentiable!
1. Reinforcment learning to optimize gating policies 2. Stochastic perturbations 3. Heuristic ‘balancing’ losses. ... Guess which one people use in practice?
RL via REINFORCE does work, but not so much better that it’s a clear win ... RL is the ‘right solution’ but gradient variances and complexity means it’s not widely used

From Shazeer et al 2017 – routing decisions are stochastic with gaussian perturbations. ... This naturally leads to experts that are a bit more robust. ... The softmax means that the model learns how to rank K experts
Stochastic jitter in Fedus et al 2022. This does a uniform multiplicative perturbation for the same goal of getting less brittle experts. This was later removed in Zoph et al 2022

anchors.ref: REINFORCE routing baseline (slide says 'Clark et al 2020')

anchors.quote: The hard thing about MoE is that during training, you only have one or k experts active. ... You only know the ones that activated. ... So it's got this RL bandit flavor to the problem, but we're not going to solve it with either RL or bandits.
And we also don't see all of the different counterfactual experts we could have picked.
if you have two experts that are closely tied or it's very close to each other, then stochastically, you'll pick one of them and not the other.
not doing any of these stochastic or robustness tricks actually helps with both stability and overall quality of the final trained MoE.

provenance.filtering_note: The REINFORCE results (p37) and the Shazeer noisy-gating equations (p38) are figures; the gaussian noise formula H(x) = (x·W_g) + StandardNormal·Softplus(x·W_noise) is not in the text. The deck does not spell out why top-k is non-differentiable (the selected set is a step function of the logits; gradients flow only through the selected gate values, so an unselected expert gets no signal) nor the straight-through alternatives. p37's 'Clark et al 2020' is the deck's year for Clark et al. 2022. Spoken evidence, which supplies what the note above says the deck omits (why top-k routing is hard to learn): 'during training, you only have one or k experts active ... You only know the ones that activated' (42:57-43:07); the gating decision is not differentiable 'and we also don't see all of the different counterfactual experts we could have picked' (59:09-59:18), a problem with a 'bandit flavor' that the field solves with heuristics instead (43:10-43:19). Spoken (1:01:36-1:02:17): what the Shazeer noise does: near-tied experts are picked stochastically, which breaks ties and explores, and helpful experts accumulate weight; the noise 'is dependent on the scale of the input'. Spoken (1:02:25-1:03:13): the later ablation found that dropping all the stochastic tricks 'actually helps with both stability and overall quality'. Spoken slip (1:00:04): 'this is from Clark 2020', repeating the deck's year on p37 (the paper is Clark et al. 2022); not imported. Straight-through estimators are not mentioned aloud.

misconceptions.belief: Because the gate weights multiply the expert outputs, backprop trains the router fully and no extra trick is needed.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Gradients reach only the gate values of the k selected experts; the decision of which experts to select is a non-differentiable argmax, and unselected experts receive no gradient at all. That is why the deck lists RL, noise and balancing losses as 'solutions'.

knowledge_points.label: Without balancing, a few experts take everything (rich get richer)
knowledge_points.statement: Plain gradient descent on a top-k router reinforces itself: chosen experts get gradient, improve, and are chosen more often, so without a balancing loss routing collapses onto a few experts (in OLMoE's 8-expert ablation almost all tokens go to two), most expert parameters are never trained, and the loss is significantly worse.

anchors.quote: So you get this rich gets richer effect, where experts that are chosen get very strong weights. ... Strong weights means that they're selected more often. ... And they run away, taking on everything.
And so this expert collapse phenomenon or expert starvation phenomenon is a very, very real problem.
But if you remove the load balancing loss, the effects are pretty catastrophic. ... Remove the load balancing loss, your losses significantly increase
Without load balancing, almost all the tokens are going to two experts ... And without it, we've thrown away a ton of parameters.
this dynamic that if an expert is useful, you're going to reinforce it. ... And that's a positive reinforcement cycle that's nicely balanced out by evening things out.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only. Slide p40 motivates balancing by 'systems efficiency', and p43 ('What happens when removing load balancing losses?') has no text layer, but its image is OLMoE's Figures 9 and 10: with no LBL, training and C4/Pile validation loss sit above the LBL run over 10B tokens, and in the first MoE layer (legend Expert 0-7, so this ablation has 8 experts) one expert briefly takes ~100% of tokens, then two experts split them roughly 50/50 while the other six get ~0; with LBL all eight sit near 12.5%. The professor gives the dynamic (1:03:24-1:04:12: 'rich gets richer', 'expert collapse ... a very, very real problem', 'the core issue'), narrates the p43 OLMoE plots (1:08:03-1:09:07: significantly higher loss, tokens going to two experts, parameters 'doing absolutely nothing'), and frames MoE training as two dynamics that cancel (1:09:34-1:09:45). This corrects the load-balancing-loss misconception note, which treated balance as a systems concern only. 'Two experts' is read off the figure, and the run has 8 experts (2/8 trained, not 2/64). The prompts' 64-expert layer is a stated hypothetical (OLMoE's released configuration on p35), not the ablation's.

prerequisites.note: Only selected experts get gradient; balancing heuristics are the chosen fix.

misconceptions.belief: Without a balancing loss, routing just ends up somewhat uneven; the model's loss is unaffected and only hardware utilization suffers.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Routing collapses onto a few experts, most expert parameters are never trained, and the loss is significantly worse (OLMoE ablation, 1:08:03-1:09:07).

misconceptions.belief: Gradient descent spreads tokens across experts by itself, because unused experts have spare capacity to offer.
misconceptions.why_wrong: An unselected expert gets no gradient, so it never improves and never wins the top-k; only chosen experts improve (1:03:35-1:03:58).

predict.targets_misconception: Gradient descent spreads tokens across experts by itself, because unused experts have spare capacity to offer.

transfer.why: Balancing is not only for hardware utilization: without it the extra parameters an MoE pays for go unused.
