knowledge_points.label: Auxiliary load-balancing loss: frequent experts get pushed down
knowledge_points.statement: Systems efficiency needs tokens spread evenly over experts, so the Switch Transformer adds an auxiliary loss α·N·Σ_i f_i·P_i (fraction of tokens routed to expert i times its mean router probability); its derivative with respect to p_i(x) is proportional to the count of tokens whose argmax is i, so the more an expert is used the harder its probability is pushed down; DeepSeek v1-2 apply this per expert and also aggregated per device.

anchors.quote: Another key issue – systems efficiency requires that we use experts evenly..
The derivative with respect to ... so more frequent use = stronger downweighting
Per-expert balancing – same as the switch transformer ... Per-device balancing – the objective above, but aggregated by device.
Standard Aux-loss balancing (Expert + Device)

anchors.ref: DeepSeekMoE expert-level and device-level balance losses

anchors.quote: this is, at least to me, not a thing, where you would derive it from first principles.
you can think of this as a penalty in the gradient space, where the more tokens you get, the more negative gradient you get.
you want those two machines to be balanced, so both of them are running at full utilization.
you don't want to crank up the per expert loss so high that you get true full uniformity, because that has deleterious effects on training dynamics.

provenance.filtering_note: The loss itself (loss = α·N·Σ f_i·P_i with f_i the fraction of tokens dispatched to expert i and P_i the mean router probability for i) is shown as an image from the Switch Transformer paper; only the derivative line is in the text, and even that comes through pdftotext as 'αN / T² Σ 1[argmax p(x) = i]' in scattered glyphs. The slide does not derive why minimizing Σ f_i P_i (with Σ f_i = Σ P_i = 1) is minimized at the uniform distribution, nor give the value of α (the Switch paper uses 10⁻²). The DeepSeek per-device objective (p41) is an image. The p43 figure 'What happens when removing load balancing losses?' has no text. Spoken evidence (1:05:02-1:05:59): the loss is 'not a thing, where you would derive it from first principles'; read it through its gradient: 'the more tokens you get, the more negative gradient you get', pushing popular experts down in proportion to their fraction. Spoken (1:06:31-1:07:11): the device term is 'just for utilization reasons', with an example of two machines holding four experts each. Spoken evidence (1:11:06-1:11:37), answering why a device term is needed when a perfectly enforced per-expert loss already balances devices: you do not want to push the per-expert loss to 'true full uniformity, because that has deleterious effects on training dynamics', but device balance is worth a little extra loss. Spoken (1:09:51-1:10:19): the same top-k-plus-auxiliary-loss trick is used in DSA and H-Nets. Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above ('The p43 figure ... has no text') and this KP's misconception note: the professor narrates p43 (1:08:03-1:09:07): without the loss 'the effects are pretty catastrophic', the loss is significantly higher and nearly all tokens go to two experts, so balancing also matters for model quality, not only for systems efficiency; see expert-collapse-without-balancing.

prerequisites.note: The balancing loss is option 3 of slide 36.

misconceptions.belief: The balancing loss pushes every expert's probability toward uniform by the same amount, however often it is used.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The derivative with respect to p_i(x) is proportional to f_i, the share of tokens routed to i (slide 40), so a heavily used expert is pushed down harder than a rarely used one: 300 vs 100 routed tokens gives a 3x stronger push. That proportionality is what makes the loss self-correcting.

misconceptions.belief: Balancing is purely a hardware concern: an unbalanced MoE reaches the same loss, it just runs slower.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The slide gives the systems reason (experts live on different devices; the step is as slow as the busiest one), but the professor's reading of the OLMoE ablation on p43 (video 1:08:03-1:09:07) is that removing the loss makes training loss 'significantly increase' while almost all tokens collapse onto a couple of experts (see expert-collapse-without-balancing). Balance matters for quality too.

predict.q: In one batch of T = 400 tokens, expert A is the argmax for 300 tokens and expert B for 100. From the derivative on slide 40, how many times stronger is the balancing loss's push-down on p_A(x) than on p_B(x)?
predict.why: The derivative with respect to p_i(x) is (αN/T²)·Σ 1[argmax p(x) = i], proportional to the number of tokens routed to i: 300 vs 100, so 3x. More frequent use = stronger downweighting.
predict.targets_misconception: The balancing loss pushes every expert's probability toward uniform by the same amount, however often it is used.

transfer.q: Experts are spread across 8 devices, 8 experts each. The per-expert loss is already near its minimum, but one device still gets twice the traffic of another. What does DeepSeek v1-2's second balancing term (slide 41) do that the first cannot?
transfer.answer: The per-device loss aggregates f_i and P_i over the experts on each device and pushes device-level loads toward uniform; the per-expert loss only constrains individual experts and can be satisfied while experts on one device are collectively hot.
transfer.why: The quantity the hardware cares about is tokens per device, since that is what each all-to-all and each FFN matmul is sized by.

check.q: Eight experts sit on 2 devices, 4 per device. The fractions of tokens each expert receives (with router probabilities matching) are 0.125, 0.25, 0.0, 0.125 on device 1 and 0.25, 0.0, 0.125, 0.125 on device 2. Which of DeepSeek v1-2's two balancing terms is far from its balanced value?
choices: neither term
only the per-device term
both terms
only the per-expert term
distractor_from: 'only the per-device term' <- plausible: reverses the aggregation, treating uneven experts as uneven devices
'both terms' <- plausible: assumes expert imbalance always shows up at the device level
'neither term' <- plausible: sees that each device's fractions sum to 0.5 and stops there, missing that individual experts range from 0 to 0.25
check.why: Per expert the loads are uneven (two experts get nothing, two get double), so the Switch-style term is high. Summed per device both get 0.5, so the device-level term, 'the objective above, but aggregated by device', is at its balanced value (p40-p41).
check.varies: the inverse of the transfer: experts unbalanced while devices are balanced
check.invariant: the device-level term sees only per-device sums of f and P; the per-expert term sees each expert

retrieval.q: What reason does the lecture give for wanting experts used evenly?
retrieval.answer: Systems efficiency.

retrieval.q: What is the derivative of the Switch balancing loss with respect to p_i(x) proportional to?
retrieval.answer: The number of tokens in the batch whose argmax expert is i (times αN/T²).

prompts.self_explain: Why does a loss built from the non-differentiable fraction f_i still produce a useful gradient on the router?

steps.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha N \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i P_i,\quad f_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_x \mathbb{1}[\arg\max p(x) = i],\quad P_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_x p_i(x)
steps.do: The Switch loss for N experts and T tokens in the batch.
steps.why: f_i, the dispatch fraction, comes from an argmax and has no gradient; P_i, the mean router probability, is differentiable. The product couples the two.

steps.tex: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}}{\partial p_i(x)} = \alpha N f_i \cdot \frac{1}{T} = \frac{\alpha N}{T^2}\sum_{x'} \mathbb{1}[\arg\max p(x') = i]
steps.do: Differentiate with respect to one token's probability for expert i: this is slide 40's derivative line.
steps.why: Only P_i contains p_i(x), with coefficient 1/T, and f_i acts as a constant. The gradient is therefore proportional to the number of tokens routed to i.

steps.do: The predict's batch: T = 400, expert A is the argmax for 300 tokens and B for 100. The push on p_A(x) is (αN/400²)·300 and on p_B(x) (αN/400²)·100: 3× stronger.
steps.why: 'More frequent use = stronger downweighting': gradient descent lowers the popular expert's probabilities fastest.

steps.do: If the router probabilities match the loads (P_i = f_i), Σ f_i² ≥ (Σ f_i)²/N = 1/N, so the loss is at least α, reached when every expert gets 1/N of the tokens.
steps.why: Cauchy-Schwarz. The slide does not derive this, but it is why minimizing the loss pulls toward a uniform load.

presentations.notice: The balancing push on each expert's probability scales with the tokens routed to it, so the hot expert is pushed down in proportion to its bar.
listen for: read the loss by its gradient: the more tokens an expert gets, the harder it is pushed down

knowledge_points.label: Aux-loss-free balancing: per-expert bias updated online (DeepSeek v3)
knowledge_points.statement: DeepSeek v3 balances load without a gradient-based auxiliary loss by adding a per-expert bias to the routing scores used for top-k selection and adjusting it online (raise the bias of under-used experts, lower it for over-used ones); the deck notes it is not fully aux-loss free because a sequence-wise auxiliary loss remains.

anchors.quote: Set up a per-expert bias (making it more likely to get tokens) and use online learning
They call this ‘auxiliary loss free balancing’ ... (but the approach is not fully aux loss free..)
Sigmoid+Softmax topK + topM ... Aux-loss-free + seq-wise aux
In DeepSeek v3, they have a per expert bias term that they use. ... but they do, in the end, have to add some of these auxiliary losses in order to ensure extreme imbalances don't happen.
there's no solution that fully gets rid of them so far.
they've switched to using sigmoid plus softmax, which is a different way of weighting their experts, but really, mostly similar.

provenance.filtering_note: The bias update rule (b_i ← b_i − γ if expert i is overloaded, b_i ← b_i + γ if underloaded, with the bias used only for selection and not for the gating weight) is in an image on p42; the text says only 'per-expert bias' and 'online learning'. The p43 comparison figure has no numbers. p56 lists 'Sigmoid+Softmax topK + topM' and 'seq-wise aux' as v3's other router changes without explanation; the sigmoid gate and the sequence-wise balance loss are in the DeepSeek-V3 report. Spoken evidence (1:07:11-1:07:52): the auxiliary loss that remains in v3 is there 'to ensure extreme imbalances don't happen', and 'there's no solution that fully gets rid of them so far'. Spoken (1:23:25-1:23:50): v3's sigmoid-plus-softmax gating is 'a different way of weighting their experts, but really, mostly similar'. The bias update rule is not described aloud.

prerequisites.note: Presented as the variation that replaces the gradient-based loss.

misconceptions.belief: The per-expert bias also scales the expert's output, so balancing changes what the model computes for a token.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The bias enters only the top-k selection score; the gating weight that multiplies the expert output still comes from the unbiased router score. Balancing moves which experts are chosen, not how their outputs are weighted.

predict.q: After a training step, expert 3 received far more tokens than average and expert 9 far fewer. Under DeepSeek v3's scheme, what happens to their biases before the next step?
choices: expert 3's bias goes down, expert 9's goes up
expert 3's bias goes up, expert 9's goes down
both are reset to zero
predict.answer: expert 3's bias goes down, expert 9's goes up
predict.why: A bias 'making it more likely to get tokens' is raised for under-used experts and lowered for over-used ones, by online update rather than by gradient. Over time this evens the load.
predict.targets_misconception: The per-expert bias also scales the expert's output, so balancing changes what the model computes for a token.

transfer.q: Name one way the bias scheme and the Switch auxiliary loss differ in how the balancing signal reaches the router, and one thing p42's parenthetical warns about the 'loss free' label.
transfer.answer: The aux loss adds a gradient term to the training objective (interfering with the language-modeling gradient); the bias is adjusted by a separate online rule outside backprop. The warning: DeepSeek v3 is 'not fully aux loss free', it keeps a sequence-wise auxiliary loss (p56).
transfer.why: The motivation for removing the loss is that its gradient competes with the LM objective; the bias achieves balance without that interference while a small residual loss handles within-sequence imbalance.

check.q: Under DeepSeek v3's scheme, expert 3's routing bias is raised so it attracts more tokens. For a token that is routed to expert 3 both before and after the change, what happens to the gate weight that multiplies expert 3's output? Answer up, down or same.
check.answer: same: the bias is added only to the scores used to choose the top-k; the gate weight comes from the original affinity, so the token's computation is unchanged.
check.why: The bias steers which experts are selected and is adjusted by an online rule outside backprop, so balancing does not change what a selected expert's output is weighted by (p42; DeepSeek-V3 §2.1.2).
check.targets_misconception: The per-expert bias also scales the expert's output, so balancing changes what the model computes for a token.
check.varies: asks about the effect on one token's output instead of how the signal reaches the router
check.invariant: the per-expert bias affects selection only, not gating weights or gradients

retrieval.answer: A per-expert bias on the routing score, updated online (not by gradient).

retrieval.q: What is the lecture's one-line caveat about 'auxiliary loss free balancing'?
retrieval.answer: The approach is not fully aux-loss free (a sequence-wise auxiliary loss remains).

knowledge_points.label: Expert parallelism: each expert fits on a device, tokens move instead
knowledge_points.statement: Because each expert FFN fits on one device, MoEs enable expert parallelism in which tokens are shuffled to the device holding their expert and back (an all-to-all), which adds communication cost and routing complexity; mitigations are block-sparse kernels such as MegaBlocks, limiting each token to M devices with a communication-balancing loss (DeepSeek v2), and down-projecting activations before sending them (Nemotron 3).

anchors.quote: MoEs parallelize nicely – Each FFN ... Enables additional kinds of parallelism ... can fit in a device
MoE routing allows for parallelism, but also some complexities ... Modern libraries like MegaBlocks (used in many open MoEs) use smarter sparse MMs
New ideas from Nemotron 3 – down-projecting the activations to reduce communication
Top-M device routing ... Communication balancing loss – balancing both communication in and out
Parallelizable to many devices

anchors.ref: DeepSeek-V2 device-limited routing and communication balance loss

anchors.quote: your experts within each FFN naturally come in different chunks. ... Each expert is a natural chunk.
You're getting more aggregate flops. ... You're reducing your memory use. ... And in exchange, you're going to pay for comms.
as you shard over more and more devices, the communication cost explodes.
I'm going to have multiple small matrix multiplies. ... But this is not nice, because you ideally want these bigger matrix multiplies
my experts, I need to communicate those activations, I want those to be in smaller lower dimensional vectors.

provenance.filtering_note: All of p44-p46 is diagrams (Switch Transformer data/model/expert parallelism grid, the dispatch/combine all-to-all, MegaBlocks' block-sparse matmul, Nemotron's down-projection); no bandwidth, token counts or speedups are in the text. The term 'all-to-all' is not used on the slides. Why dense batched matmuls are awkward for MoE (each expert receives a different, data-dependent number of tokens, forcing padding or dropping) is the implied motivation for MegaBlocks' 'smarter sparse MMs' but is not stated. The p55 'Top-M device routing' limits each token's experts to M devices; M is not given in the text. Spoken evidence (41:57-42:33), in Q&A: expert parallelism trades 'more aggregate flops' and less memory per device for communication, so whether it is a net win 'is highly dependent on your topology'; it has an upper limit because 'the communication cost explodes' as devices are added (44:00), which the assignment works through (44:09). Spoken (1:12:17-1:12:42): why another axis helps: data parallelism stops at the batch size, model parallelism at the model's natural cut points. Spoken evidence, which partly supplies the motivation the note above calls unstated: several experts on one GPU run as many small matmuls 'is not nice, because you ideally want these bigger matrix multiplies'; block-diagonal or structured sparse matmuls fix that (1:12:54-1:13:47). Spoken imprecision (1:12:42, 1:13:17): he says this uses 'sparse matrix multiply that has been built into GPUs' and structured sparsity 'natively supported in hardware'; the slide says only 'smarter sparse MMs', and MegaBlocks' block-sparse kernels are software kernels on dense tensor cores rather than the GPU's 2:4 structured-sparsity feature (author's note; not imported). Spoken (1:13:55-1:14:54): the Nemotron 3 trick: keep the shared expert at full width, down-project only the routed experts' activations before the collective, saving communication 'without fully having the drawbacks of having a smaller hidden dimension size'. DeepSeek v2's device routing and communication loss are 'adding auxiliary losses to optimize systems' (1:22:58-1:23:11). 'All-to-all' is not said aloud.

prerequisites.note: Device-level balance (p41) is the per-device version of this concern.

external_prerequisites.note: Communication bytes per token vs expert FLOPs per token is the ratio that decides whether expert parallelism is network-bound.

misconceptions.why_wrong: Weights stay put; it is the token activations that are sent to the expert's device and the outputs sent back. That is why communication scales with tokens × hidden size, and why Nemotron 3's down-projection of activations and DeepSeek v2's cap of M devices per token reduce it.

knowledge_points.label: Token dropping at the batch level makes MoE outputs depend on other requests
knowledge_points.statement: When an expert receives more tokens than its capacity, the excess tokens are dropped from that expert (they pass through the residual only); since routing and capacity are decided per batch, whether your token is dropped depends on what other sequences in the batch routed to the same expert, which adds stochasticity to MoE inference that dense models do not have.

anchors.quote: MoEs can have additional stochasticity beyond normal models.. ... Why would a MoE have additional randomness?
Token dropping from routing happens at a batch level – this means that other people’s queries can drop your token!

anchors.quote: my queue is so long, I have to start dropping tokens.
you would just actually silently drop this expert. ... You just send a zero back and pretend that that was fine.
if other users sent in queries that hit the experts that you're using, then you could actually get a worse result, because they would bump you out of the expert queue.
But these days, they drop less architectures that have gotten rid of a lot of these issues. ... So mega blocks and other very common open source MoE frameworks don't have this issue anymore.

provenance.filtering_note: The slide never says 'capacity factor' or defines expert capacity (Switch Transformer: capacity = (tokens in batch / number of experts) × capacity factor, with tokens beyond it dropped); the mechanism is only implied by 'token dropping from routing'. The p47 figure (a tweet or forum screenshot about nondeterministic outputs) has no text. Dropless alternatives (MegaBlocks on p45) are not connected to this slide by the deck. The balance between capacity factor, padding waste and drop rate is not discussed. Spoken evidence (1:15:17-1:16:18): the mechanism told as a queue: a popular expert's token queue builds up until tokens are dropped; older inference code would 'silently drop' them and 'send a zero back' (consistent with the statement: the expert contributes zero and only the residual remains), so other users' queries could 'bump you out of the expert queue'. Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above ('Dropless alternatives ... are not connected to this slide by the deck'): the professor connects them aloud: 'these days, they drop less architectures ... mega blocks and other very common open source MoE frameworks don't have this issue anymore' (1:16:21-1:16:35), and calls the topic 'trivia ... solved in recent years' (1:15:07). Capacity factor is not named aloud.

prerequisites.note: Dropping is what happens when balance fails at the batch level.
Fixed per-expert buffers exist because each expert's device allocates a fixed tensor per step.

misconceptions.belief: If the average load per expert is below capacity, no tokens are dropped.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Capacity is per expert per batch; a popular expert can overflow while others sit nearly empty even when the mean is fine. Dropping is a tail event of the load distribution, which is why balance (not just average utilization) matters.

predict.q: A batch of 512 tokens, 8 experts, top-1, capacity 96 tokens per expert (so 768 slots total, far above 512). The router sends 150 tokens to expert 2 and spreads the rest evenly. How many tokens are dropped?
predict.why: Expert 2 overflows by 150 − 96 = 54; the other 7 experts hold 362/7 ≈ 52 each, under capacity. Total slots were plenty, yet 54 tokens skip the FFN. Average load does not protect you.
predict.targets_misconception: If the average load per expert is below capacity, no tokens are dropped.

transfer.q: You send the same prompt twice to an MoE served with batch-level capacity limits and get different completions, with temperature 0. Which slide-47 mechanism explains this, and what would make the result deterministic?
transfer.answer: Other requests in the batch routed to the same experts and pushed some of your tokens over capacity, so they were dropped in one run and not the other. Serving with batch size 1, with a dropless (MegaBlocks-style) kernel, or with capacity large enough that nothing overflows removes the dependence.
transfer.why: Greedy decoding is deterministic only if the forward pass is; batch-level dropping makes the forward pass a function of the co-batched requests.

check.q: Top-1 routing with a capacity of 64 tokens per expert, and the batch's average load per expert is well below 64. In this batch your request routes 40 tokens to expert 5 and another request in the same batch routes 50 tokens to expert 5. How many tokens are dropped at expert 5? Type only the number.
check.why: Expert 5 receives 40 + 50 = 90 tokens for 64 slots, so 26 are dropped; the average load does not matter. Alone, your 40 tokens would all fit, so whether your tokens are dropped depends on who else is in the batch (p47).
check.targets_misconception: If the average load per expert is below capacity, no tokens are dropped.
check.varies: explicit co-batched counts instead of an observed nondeterminism
check.invariant: capacity is enforced per expert per batch, so other requests' routing decides what is dropped

retrieval.q: The same prompt sent twice to an MoE model at temperature 0 gives different outputs. Which MoE mechanism can explain this, and how?
retrieval.answer: Token dropping: expert capacity is decided per batch, so other requests routed to the same expert can push your token over capacity and drop it.

retrieval.q: What happens to a token that is dropped by an expert?
retrieval.answer: It is not processed by that expert (it continues through the residual stream without that FFN's contribution).

prompts.self_explain: Why does dropping, rather than queueing, the overflow tokens follow from how the expert buffers are laid out on a device?

presentations.notice: The hot expert overflows while the mean line sits below capacity; raising only the other requests' tokens decides whether your tokens are dropped.

knowledge_points.label: Router stability: float32 router and the z-loss
knowledge_points.statement: MoE training can diverge because the router's softmax is sensitive to large logits; the fix is to compute the router (just the router) in float32 and optionally add a z-loss that penalizes the log of the softmax normalizer so router logits stay small.

anchors.quote: Solution: Use Float 32 just for the expert router (sometimes with an aux z-loss)
Z-loss stability for the router ... What happens when we remove the z-loss?
Training objectives are somewhat heuristic (and sometimes unstable)

anchors.ref: ST-MoE §3 router z-loss and float32 routing

anchors.quote: I said exponentials are bad, divisions are bad, which means softmaxes are danger zone for stability issues.
we have introduced yet another softmax in the routing
It's quite clear, from these very spiky training loss curves, that z-loss on the router can be quite helpful.

provenance.filtering_note: The z-loss formula L_z = (1/B) Σ (log Σ_j exp(x_j))² and the instability plots are images from Zoph 2022 (p48-p49); no formula or loss values are in the text. The slide does not explain why the router specifically is fragile (exp of bf16 logits with large magnitude overflows or loses precision, and small logit noise flips the discrete top-k choice) or that the z-loss was later adopted for the output softmax of dense models too. Whether 'sometimes' means optional in practice is left open. Spoken evidence (1:16:42-1:17:10): the reason, recalled from lecture 3: 'exponentials are bad, divisions are bad, which means softmaxes are danger zone', and routing adds 'yet another softmax'. Spoken (1:17:49-1:18:11): the z-loss 'was quite popular ... to do MoE router stability even in the early days', and the p49 OLMoE ablation shows 'very spiky training loss curves' without it. The overflow mechanism and the top-k flip are still not stated aloud.

prerequisites.note: Discrete selection is what turns small logit error into a large change in computation.

external_prerequisites.note: Why float32 vs bf16 matters for exp of large logits.
The router is the one piece kept in fp32 inside an otherwise bf16 model.
Same penalty on the log-normaliser, applied here to the router softmax instead of the output softmax.

misconceptions.belief: Running the router in float32 makes MoE training much slower.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The router is a single small linear layer and softmax per token (hidden × number of experts); its cost is negligible beside the experts, which stay in bf16. The slide stresses 'just for the expert router'.

predict.q: An MoE in bf16 diverges mid-training with router logits growing large. Per slide 48, what is the first change to make, and roughly how much does it change total training FLOPs?
choices: compute only the router in float32; negligible FLOP change
compute the whole model in float32; about 2x the bytes and time
halve the learning rate for the experts
predict.answer: compute only the router in float32; negligible FLOP change
predict.why: Slide 48: 'Use Float 32 just for the expert router (sometimes with an aux z-loss)'. The router is tiny relative to the experts, so precision there is nearly free.
predict.targets_misconception: Running the router in float32 makes MoE training much slower.

transfer.q: The z-loss penalizes (log Σ_j exp x_j)² on the router logits. If all logits shift up by a constant c, what happens to the softmax probabilities and to the z-loss, and why does that make it a stability term rather than a quality term?
transfer.answer: Probabilities are unchanged (softmax is shift-invariant); the z-loss grows with c. So it pulls the logits toward a scale near zero without changing the routing distribution, keeping exp() in a numerically safe range.
transfer.why: Instability came from the magnitude of the logits, not their relative values; a penalty that is blind to the routing decision but sensitive to magnitude targets exactly that.

check.q: A router scores 8 experts and every logit equals the same value c. The router z-loss is (log Σ_j exp x_j)². For what value of c is the z-loss exactly zero? Type only the number.
check.why: log Σ exp(c) = c + ln 8, which is 0 at c = −ln 8 ≈ −2.08. The routing probabilities are 1/8 for every c, because softmax is shift-invariant: the z-loss picks the logit scale without touching the routing distribution (p48-p49).
check.varies: a specific logit vector and the zero point instead of a qualitative shift
check.invariant: the z-loss depends on the logits' overall level, the softmax only on their differences

retrieval.q: Why is the router the one MoE component that must run in float32?
retrieval.answer: Its softmax is sensitive to large logits, so low-precision router logits can make training diverge.

retrieval.q: What does the z-loss penalize?
retrieval.answer: The (squared) log of the router softmax normalizer, i.e. large router logits.

prompts.self_explain: Why would a small numerical error in the router hurt more than the same error in an expert's weights?

presentations.notice: listen for: why the router is fragile: it adds another softmax, and softmaxes are the danger zone

knowledge_points.label: Upcycling: initialize an MoE from a pretrained dense model
knowledge_points.statement: Upcycling builds an MoE from a pretrained dense LM by copying its FFN into each expert and adding a router, then continuing training; MiniCPM did this with top-k=2, 8 experts (~4B active) and ~520B tokens, and Qwen MoE from Qwen 1.8B with top-k=4, 60 experts and 4 shared, one of the first confirmed successes.

anchors.quote: Can we use a pre-trained LM to initialize a MoE?
Uses the MiniCPM model (topk=2, 8 experts, ~ 4B active params). ... Simple MoE, shows gains from the base model with ~ 520B tokens for training
Qwen MoE – Initialized from the Qwen 1.8B model top-k=4, 60 experts w/ 4 shared. ... Similar architecture / setup to DeepSeekMoE, but one of the first (confirmed) upcycling successes
This has actually become a lot less popular in the last year. ... I don't think I've seen a single upcycled model this year.
You have a router, which have a random initialization. ... because of the stochasticity of which inputs go to where and the MLP, you're going to get these experts that start to specialize.
They upcycled it to a 13.4 billion parameter model.
you don't really train dense models and then convert them. ... You might as well just train your big hero run on an MoE to start with.

provenance.filtering_note: The upcycling diagram on p51 (dense checkpoint's MLP copied into every expert, router initialized fresh) is an image; the copy-the-FFN recipe is not stated in the text and comes from the cited paper. MiniCPM's and Qwen MoE's result tables (p52-p53) are figures without numbers in the text. Since experts start identical, what breaks the symmetry (router noise, different token subsets) is not discussed. Qwen 1.5's 60 routed / 4 shared matches the p35 table row. Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above (symmetry breaking 'not discussed'): the copies start identical, and the randomly initialized router plus 'the stochasticity of which inputs go to where' make the experts 'start to specialize' (1:20:18-1:20:32). Spoken (1:19:46-1:19:53, 1:21:46-1:21:59): upcycling has 'become a lot less popular ... I don't think I've seen a single upcycled model this year', because big runs now train an MoE from the start. Spoken numbers not in the slide text: MiniCPM's 2.4B dense model upcycled 'to a 13.4 billion parameter model' (1:21:11-1:21:18; a spoken slip: the p52 table says MiniCPM-MoE (13.6B)), and Qwen 1.8B upcycled to 'Qwen 1.5.A, 2.7B' (1:21:24-1:21:37; 2.7B active, consistent with Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B). The earliest upcycling paper beat continued dense training (1:20:35-1:20:59).

prerequisites.note: Qwen MoE's upcycled architecture is 'similar to DeepSeekMoE'.

misconceptions.belief: An upcycled MoE with 8 experts starts with 8 different specialists taken from the dense model.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The dense model has one FFN per layer, so all 8 experts begin as identical copies; specialization has to emerge during the continued training (hundreds of billions of tokens in MiniCPM's case).

predict.q: Right after upcycling a dense model into an 8-expert top-2 MoE (before any further training), how does the MoE layer's output on a token compare with the dense FFN's output?
choices: identical up to the gate weights, since all experts are copies of the same FFN
8 different outputs mixed, since each expert came from a different layer
random, since the experts are re-initialized
predict.answer: identical up to the gate weights, since all experts are copies of the same FFN
predict.why: Every expert equals the original FFN, so top-2 selection returns two copies of the same function weighted by the gate (summing to the dense output when gates sum to 1). Divergence between experts comes only from subsequent training.
predict.targets_misconception: An upcycled MoE with 8 experts starts with 8 different specialists taken from the dense model.

transfer.q: Using the slide-53 configuration (Qwen 1.8B dense → 60 routed experts, top-4, 4 shared) and assuming every expert is a copy of the dense FFN, what factor on FFN parameters does the upcycled model have, and what factor on active FFN compute per token?
transfer.answer: 64x the FFN parameters (60 routed + 4 shared copies); 8x the active FFN compute (4 routed + 4 shared experts run per token) if experts are full-size copies.
transfer.why: This is why Qwen MoE then shrinks experts to fine-grained size (p35 lists its ratio as 1/8), which brings active compute back near the dense model while keeping many parameters. The slide gives only the counts; the sizing follows from the DeepSeekMoE-style design it says Qwen adopted.

check.q: A dense model is upcycled into an MoE with 16 routed experts (top-2) plus 1 shared expert, every expert a full copy of the dense FFN. Relative to the dense FFN, by what factor is the active FFN compute per token multiplied? Type only the number.
check.why: Each token runs 2 routed experts plus the shared one: 3 full-size FFNs. Parameters are 17x the dense FFN. Upcycling copies the FFN; only the experts that run cost compute (p51-p53).
check.varies: different expert, top-k and shared counts; asks one factor
check.invariant: active compute counts experts run per token (routed top-k plus shared) times expert size

retrieval.q: State the MiniCPM upcycling configuration (k, experts, active params, training tokens).
retrieval.answer: top-k = 2, 8 experts, about 4B active parameters, about 520B tokens.

retrieval.q: From which dense model was Qwen MoE upcycled, with how many experts and shared experts?
retrieval.answer: Qwen 1.8B; 60 experts with 4 shared, top-k = 4.

retrieval.q: When a pretrained dense LM is upcycled into an MoE, how are the experts and the router set up before training continues?
retrieval.answer: Each expert starts as a copy of the dense model's FFN and a new router is added; then training continues.

prompts.self_explain: Why would starting from identical experts still be a better initialization than random experts, given that the router has to learn to tell them apart?

presentations.notice: With full-size copies (size 1) every routed and shared expert that runs costs one dense FFN, so active compute is k + shared while parameters are E + shared.

knowledge_points.label: MLA: cache a low-dimensional latent instead of K and V
knowledge_points.statement: Multi-head latent attention expresses Q, K and V as linear functions of a lower-dimensional latent c_t, so the KV cache stores only c_t^KV (much smaller than full K and V) and the key up-projection W^UK can be merged into the query projection; RoPE conflicts with this because the rotation sits between W^Q and W^UK, so DeepSeek keeps a few non-latent key dimensions that are rotated.

anchors.quote: MLA : Multihead, latent attention ... Basic idea: express the Q, K, V as functions of a lower-dim, ‘latent’ activation
Benefits: when KV-caching, we only need to store ... which can be much smaller. ... can be merged into the Q projection ... (they also compress queries, for memory savings during training)
Complexity: rope conflicts with MLA-style caching. ... The solution – Have a few non-latent key dimensions that can be rotated
Instead of KB cashing all your Ks and Vs, I only need to store these Cs.
this is going to conflict with rope when you do KB caching.
the trick is, you have nonlatent dimensions that encode positions, but I'm not going to go into too much more details about that.

provenance.filtering_note: The MLA diagram (p57) and the projection equations are images; the text gives only the two inner-product lines on p58 (without RoPE ⟨h W^Q W^UK, c^KV⟩ can absorb W^UK into the query side; with RoPE the rotation matrices R_q, R_k sit between W^Q and W^UK and cannot be merged). The latent dimension (d_c = 512 in DeepSeek-V2 vs 128 heads × 128 dims) and the size of the decoupled RoPE key (64 dims) are not in the text. The deck does not compare MLA against MQA/GQA (lecture 3) and does not give the KV-cache-bytes formula; see supp-kv-cache-bytes. p59 (MTP: 'small, lightweight models that predict multiple steps ahead', 'they only do MTP with one token ahead', cited next to EAGLE) is the last DeepSeek v3 ingredient and is left as context. Spoken evidence (1:23:59-1:25:04): MLA comes as part of the DeepSeek v3 walkthrough; the cache stores the latent c because it is 'hopefully, lower dimensional'; the RoPE conflict is named and the decoupled-RoPE fix is explicitly skipped: 'you have nonlatent dimensions that encode positions, but I'm not going to go into too much more details about that' (1:24:56). The absorption of W^UK into the query projection (p58) is not explained aloud. MTP (p59) is 'a speculative decoder built in', deferred to the inference lecture (1:25:25-1:25:40).

prerequisites.note: Both are answers to the growing KV cache; MLA shrinks what is cached per token, the recurrent form makes it constant.
To size the saving you need the per-token KV-cache formula the deck assumes.

misconceptions.belief: MLA saves KV-cache memory by using fewer attention heads, like MQA/GQA.
misconceptions.why_wrong: MLA keeps all heads; it caches a single low-rank latent c_t^KV per token from which every head's K and V are reconstructed by up-projection (or absorbed into the query). The saving comes from the latent width being far smaller than heads × head_dim × 2, not from sharing heads.

predict.q: With MLA and no RoPE, the key up-projection W^UK can be merged into the query projection. Where does RoPE have to be applied for this merge to break, according to slide 58?
choices: between W^Q and W^UK, so the rotation sits inside the merged product
on the value vectors, so the rotation passes into the output projection
after the attention softmax, so the rotation reweights the scores
predict.answer: between W^Q and W^UK, so the rotation sits inside the merged product
distractor_from: 'on the value vectors' <- plausible: confuses the W^UK-into-query absorption with the W^UV-into-output absorption
'after the softmax' <- plausible: treats RoPE as a score-level position bias (ALiBi-style) rather than a rotation of q and k
predict.why: Without RoPE the score is ⟨h W^Q W^UK, c^KV⟩ and W^Q W^UK is one matrix. With RoPE it is ⟨h W^Q R_q, R_k W^UK c^KV⟩; the position-dependent R_q R_k sits between the two weights, so you cannot precompute their product. The fix is a few non-latent key dimensions that carry the rotation.
predict.targets_misconception: MLA saves KV-cache memory by using fewer attention heads, like MQA/GQA.

transfer.q: A layer has 128 heads of dimension 128. Full K and V caching stores 2 × 128 × 128 = 32768 values per token per layer. MLA caches a 512-dim latent plus a 64-dim rotated key. By what factor does per-token cache shrink (ignoring bytes per value)?
transfer.why: 32768 / (512 + 64) ≈ 56.9x. The latent and RoPE sizes here are DeepSeek-V2's and are not on the slide; the deck says only 'much smaller'. At any precision the ratio is the same because both sides use the same dtype.

retrieval.q: Besides shrinking the KV cache, what does writing K as a linear function of the latent c_t let MLA do with the key up-projection W^UK?
retrieval.answer: Merge it into the query projection, so full keys need not be materialised.

retrieval.q: What complication does RoPE create for MLA, and what is DeepSeek's solution?
retrieval.answer: RoPE conflicts with MLA-style caching (the rotation blocks merging W^UK into the query); solution: keep a few non-latent key dimensions that can be rotated.

prompts.self_explain: Why can W^UK be folded into the query side at all, and why does that fold save compute at decode time?

steps.do: MLA caches the latent c^KV for each token and rebuilds keys from it with the up-projection W^UK; queries come from h W^Q.
steps.why: Only the low-dimensional latent is stored per token, which is the saving (p58: 'much smaller').

steps.do: Without RoPE, move W^UK to the query side.
steps.why: W^Q W^UK is a product of two fixed matrices, so it can be precomputed as one query projection, and scores are taken against the cached latent without materializing any key.

steps.do: With RoPE, the rotations sit between W^Q and W^UK.
steps.why: R_q and R_k depend on the positions of the two tokens, so the matrix between h and c^KV changes for every pair and cannot be folded into one fixed projection.

steps.do: The fix on p58: a few extra non-latent key dimensions carry the rotation, and the latent part stays unrotated and mergeable.
steps.why: Position goes into a small side channel, so the cache holds the latent plus a short rotated key instead of full K and V.

presentations.notice: Ticking MLA swaps 2 · heads · head_dim values per layer for latent + rotated-key width, without dropping any heads; the shrink factor is the same at every dtype and context length.
listen for: what MLA caches instead of K and V, and why that is smaller

external_prerequisites.note: MLA is the alternative to sharing K/V heads: all heads kept, one latent cached.

knowledge_points.label: Supplement: KV-cache bytes per token = 2 · layers · heads · head_dim · bytes
knowledge_points.statement: Softmax attention at decode time must keep every past token's key and value for every layer and head, so the cache costs 2 · n_layers · n_kv_heads · head_dim · bytes_per_value per token and grows linearly with context; this is the cost that linear attention (constant state), hybrids (fewer softmax layers), MQA/GQA (fewer KV heads) and MLA (a small latent) each attack differently.

anchors.quote: Benefits: when KV-caching, we only need to store ... which can be much smaller.
inference efficiently (using the serial, linear form)
Cost of attention rises with large context sizes… how do we control those costs?
Instead of KB cashing all your Ks and Vs, I only need to store these Cs.

provenance.filtering_note: Not in this lecture: the deck assumes the learner knows what a KV cache is and why it grows (p2's figure, p5's 'inference efficiently', p58's 'when KV-caching'). The formula is the student line's addition so the linear-attention, hybrid and MLA KPs can be quantified; MQA/GQA, the other standard remedy, are taught in lecture 3 (lecture_03:mqa-gqa-kv-cache) and are not in this deck at all. n_kv_heads equals n_heads for standard multi-head attention. Spoken (9:07-9:16, 1:24:25-1:24:30): the professor contrasts linear attention's fixed-size state and MLA's latent with caching 'all your Ks and Vs', but never states the per-token formula aloud; it remains the student line's addition.

external_prerequisites.note: Decode reads the whole cache per generated token, which is why cache bytes, not FLOPs, bound long-context decoding.
Lecture 3 gives the KV-cache motivation and the n_kv_heads factor; this supplement states the full product.

misconceptions.belief: The KV cache is a fixed cost like the weights; it does not depend on how long the conversation is.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Every generated or prompted token adds 2·L·H·d·bytes to the cache, so at long context the cache can exceed the weights. That growth, not the weights, is what the alternatives in this lecture target.

predict.q: A model has 32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim 128, bf16 (2 bytes). What is the KV-cache size per token, in bytes?
predict.why: 2 (K and V) × 32 layers × 32 heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes = 512 KiB per token. A 32k-token context is 16 GiB of cache, before any batching.
predict.targets_misconception: The KV cache is a fixed cost like the weights; it does not depend on how long the conversation is.

transfer.q: Same model, but as a 3-1 hybrid where only 8 of the 32 layers are softmax attention (the rest keep a fixed-size state). What is the KV cache for a 32k-token context, in GiB, ignoring the fixed states?
transfer.why: Per token: 2 × 8 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes; × 32,768 tokens = 4 GiB, a quarter of the dense model's 16 GiB. Each alternative in the lecture edits one factor: hybrids cut layers, GQA cuts heads, MLA cuts heads × head_dim to a latent width, linear attention removes the per-token term entirely.

retrieval.q: In the per-token KV-cache size 2 · layers · kv_heads · head_dim · bytes, which factor does each of hybrids, GQA and MLA reduce?
retrieval.answer: Hybrids: the number of layers with a cache. GQA/MQA: n_kv_heads. MLA: replaces n_kv_heads · head_dim · 2 with a latent width.

retrieval.q: Why does the KV cache grow with context while the recurrent state of linear attention does not?
retrieval.answer: Softmax attention needs every past key and value to compute the normalizer and weighted sum; the recurrence folds them into one d_k × d_v matrix.

prompts.self_explain: Why does the factor 2 appear in the formula, and which of the lecture's alternatives removes it rather than shrinking the other factors?

presentations.notice: Cache per token is softmax layers × KV heads × head_dim × 2 (or the MLA latent width) × bytes; the total grows linearly with context in every design while the per-token size does not.

steps.do: Per token, per layer, per KV head: one key and one value of head_dim each, 2 × 128 = 256 values (the predict's model).
steps.why: Decoding attends to every past token's key and value, so both have to be kept.

steps.do: × 32 heads × 32 layers: 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 = 262,144 values per token.
steps.why: Every layer has its own K and V for every KV head; n_kv_heads = n_heads for standard multi-head attention.

steps.do: × 2 bytes per value in bf16.
steps.why: bytes_per_value is the dtype width (lecture_02:dtype-bytes).

steps.do: × a 32,768-token context: 524,288 × 32,768 = 2^34 bytes = 16 GiB for one sequence.
steps.why: The cache grows linearly with context, and each alternative in the lecture attacks one factor of the product.
